project.title: ECC Challenges
project.html:
ECC Challenges

A public, distributed Pollard rho search on the Certicom ECC challenges: 24 elliptic-curve discrete logarithm problems from 79 to 359 bits. Ten were solved between 1997 and 2004; fourteen remain open. Workers walk a curve and send back distinguished points (DPs), the walk positions that satisfy a sparse predicate. The server checks every point and looks for a collision between any two walks.

Take part in three steps

  1. Sign in with GitHub at ecc-challenges.com and create an API key. The key is shown once; the installers below save it for you, or keep it in ~/.config/ecc-challenges/api-key with mode 0600.

  2. Start one worker on the machine you have:

    Machine Command
    Linux with Docker, CPU or NVIDIA GPU the docker run command on your dashboard
    Linux without Docker, or a Mac (Metal) curl -fsSL https://ecc-challenges.com/install.sh | sh
    Windows, in PowerShell irm https://ecc-challenges.com/install.ps1 | iex

    Choose the challenge with ECC_CAMPAIGN; the installers default to eccp-131. Keep the worker's data directory between restarts. It holds the run identity and checkpoint.

  3. Check that it reports. Within a few minutes the run appears on your dashboard with its heartbeat, uploads and verification state, and in the active count on the status page.

Running a worker has the full recipes: Docker, Compose, Kubernetes, systemd, Podman, Slurm/Apptainer, Modal, macOS and Windows, on GPU (CUDA, Metal) or CPU (x86-64 and arm64). A coding agent can do the setup: agent setup has a prompt and the reusable worker skill. If something goes wrong, see help.

To work on the code, read CONTRIBUTING.md and the open problems. The local stack runs the whole platform on one machine. Live numbers are on the status page and at /v1/status.

How the gateway is built

ecc-challenges.com is the contribution gateway for the 24 published Certicom ECC challenges. A contributor signs in with GitHub, creates a revocable API key, and runs a pinned Linux container on a workstation or cloud provider. The generic v2 worker handles prime and binary fields up to 359 bits. Its CPU, NVIDIA CUDA and Apple Metal backends share one arithmetic core (worker/generic/ec_core.h) and run on Linux, macOS and Windows. Existing ecc2k-130 v1 state keeps its original Frobenius walk and 32-byte record format.

Release status

All 24 curves were enabled on the public gateway on 19 October 2026. The final CPU image passed all-curve checks natively on amd64 and arm64. The final combined CPU/CUDA image passed 336 checks on a RunPod RTX 4090. Bounded live CPU checks passed registration, independently checked checkpoint witnesses, same-run restart and closure on every curve. Short runs emitted production points on ECC2-79 and ECCp-79. These checks do not establish point rates on larger curves or fleet capacity. All validation pods were terminated. See the release receipts and earlier correctness controls.

Two public worker images are built from this repository:

Image Hardware
ecc-challenges-worker Linux amd64 CPU or NVIDIA CUDA
ecc-challenges-worker-cpu Linux amd64 and arm64 CPU

Each image supports all 24 curves. Always run the immutable digest shown on your dashboard or in /v1/campaigns; the gateway publishes digests only, never a moving tag. FPGA acceleration is deferred.

A v2 worker uploads immutable, checksum-bound batches directly to versioned S3. The server verifies every point relation and conditionally indexes exact points in DynamoDB. PostgreSQL holds identity, quotas, admission cursors and processing metadata. See the all-curve storage design for namespace binding, sizing, collision safety, compaction and archive reconstruction.

flowchart LR
  GPU[Worker: CPU or GPU container] -->|API key, small control JSON| ALB[WAF + HTTPS ALB]
  ALB --> API[Stateless API tasks]
  GPU -->|checksum-bound direct PUT| S3[Versioned immutable S3 archive]
  API -->|namespace and admission receipts| S3
  API -->|identity, quotas, cursor, outbox| PG[(Private PostgreSQL)]
  PG -->|durable delivery and repair| SQS[Audit queue]
  SQS --> Audit[Full v2 point verification]
  S3 -->|pinned raw version| Audit
  Audit --> Index[Conditional DynamoDB point index]
  Index --> Resolver[Coefficient collision + scalar check]
  Resolver -->|immutable result| S3

The diagram shows v2. The separate legacy ecc2k-130 protocol keeps its sampled trail replay and PostgreSQL candidate projection. Historical points are imported one way by scripts/historical_import.py (see operations). New generic points have their own curve and walk namespaces.

Running GPU workers

Run one container per GPU. Set ECC_GPU to the device index (the dashboard command takes it from a GPU_ID shell variable) and give each GPU its own persistent data directory. Never restart a run with a fresh directory while its earlier seed range is active. On Linux, install the NVIDIA Container Toolkit so Docker's --gpus all can expose the card. For an RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell worker in your own Modal account, follow the Modal worker guide. Start with one bounded worker and check its registration, upload, replay and index status before adding more.

The container pauses collection when the local upload spool reaches its limit and retries with the same run ID. A server 429 or 503 means back off; do not discard the local file. Revoking the key stops uploads for its runs. A key is not an AWS credential. It grants no bucket listing, archive reads or database access, and a signed upload capability permits only its one bounded object write.

What an accepted upload means

For v2, admission checks key and account limits, UUID ownership, namespace, cursor, record alignment and checksum-bound S3 object metadata. Its acknowledgment means the versioned raw bytes and the admission receipt are durable. The audit worker then checks every record's DP predicate, curve equation and R=aG+bQ relation before any DynamoDB insertion. A collision rechecks its source receipts and coefficient witnesses, computes the candidate scalar and checks dG=Q. Verified coefficient relations do not attest reported trail lengths, so the site's work and completion figures are estimates from point counts (docs/campaigns.md), not verified work.

The separate legacy ecc2k-130 sigma protocol accepts DP30, DP32 and DP34 (the number is the DP threshold in bits). The NVIDIA dashboard recommends DP34 for new runs; existing runs keep their threshold. See threshold selection.

The API checks framing, run ID, canonical orbit-key shape at the run's threshold, body size, cursor, key status, key rate and quota, and global pending capacity. It stores the exact bytes under a checksum-bound, write-once S3 key. A successful upload acknowledges archival and the committed cursor. It does not assert that each record came from the claimed seed.

The first batch of each run is selected for independent replay. Later batches are selected after sealing with probability 1/128. A passing first replay opens indexing for that run; sampled and unselected states stay distinct. All public points are kept in ecc_public.candidate_points, separate from the existing campaign's authoritative table. A failed later replay suspends the run, revokes its key, disqualifies already indexed candidate points and quarantines its leads. A collision lead triggers exact replay of both trails and a pinned host solver. A separate golden-model multiplication must also check the reported scalar against the challenge points before the lead is marked verified.

These checks contain abuse and preserve evidence, but sparse random sampling cannot certify every point in a batch. The service still relies on quotas, queue backpressure, operator monitoring and exact replay of every collision lead.

Development

uv sync --extra test
# Needs PostgreSQL 16 binaries on PATH (initdb, pg_ctl), or set TEST_POSTGRES_DSN.
# macOS: PATH=/opt/homebrew/opt/postgresql@16/bin:$PATH
uv run python -m pytest -q
aws cloudformation validate-template --template-body file://infra/foundation.yaml
aws cloudformation validate-template --template-body file://infra/data.yaml
aws cloudformation validate-template --template-body file://infra/service.yaml

The integration suite starts isolated PostgreSQL and mocked S3 and SQS. It checks key lifecycle, run assignment, upload idempotency, archival, outbox repair, indexing, failed-replay quarantine and the HTTP worker protocol. The audit image builds and runs the pinned arithmetic test before copying the replay binary; its host solver is separately built from a pinned crypto source commit. Source bundles and hashes are under vendor/.

Deployment and capacity

Operations covers image publishing, AWS stacks, Squarespace DNS, GitHub OAuth setup, rollout checks and queue alarms. Admission and capacity covers the threat model, rate limits and the measurable throughput gate. The capacity script takes observed rates:

python3 scripts/capacity.py --gpus 1000 --steps-per-gpu-second 1000000000 \
  --steps-per-dp 350000000 --index-rows-per-task-second 20000 \
  --audit-seconds-per-record 600 --new-runs-per-hour 100

The numbers in that command are illustrative input, not campaign measurements. Opening the site to a large fleet requires a measured replay time and a sustained arrival and drain test. The capacity problem record tracks both.

Source and campaign boundary

The worker GPU base is the immutable image ghcr.io/aburan28/ecc2k130-worker@sha256:25299db686c6b73bb59edc1b5f6591d917ada4e5d933172a4eca7274a71e9421. The replay source is aburan28/cryptanalysis commit c8cc56d8c98705c7f84a21aae1e042453e0105e6; the scalar resolver source is aburan28/crypto commit 79006eb85a400474e83f6a76fac0dca6b60a8b5d. The isolated S3 seed registry is the admission authority for public run IDs. The original campaign table stays in its own account, and this service never writes to it. Until its points are imported and backmatched, collision lookup covers new public candidates only. The paper's quantitative claims go through the paper's separate evidence and submission process.

contributing.title: Contributing
contributing.html:
Contributing

There are two ways to help: run a worker, or work on the code.

Run a worker

Sign in at ecc-challenges.com, create an API key and run the docker run command your dashboard shows. Running a worker covers every other setup: CPU-only, Compose, Kubernetes, systemd, Podman, Slurm and Modal. If something looks wrong, such as rejected uploads, a crash or a number on the status page that does not add up, open an issue with the worker log. Never paste your API key.

Work on the code

Layout

Path What it is
src/ecc_challenges/ FastAPI website and worker API (app.py), templates, status page
src/ecc_challenges/multicurve/ v2 protocol for all 24 curves: codec, admission, verification, index
worker/ Worker client and generic CPU/CUDA/Metal engine. generic/ec_core.h is the shared reference core; generic/fast131.h is the specialized 131-bit arithmetic and batched walks; CMakeLists.txt builds both on Linux, macOS and Windows. Dockerfile (GPU) and Dockerfile.cpu (CPU, amd64 and arm64) build the images. tests/ runs on every platform with only pytest
deploy/ Ways to run workers (Compose, Kubernetes, systemd, Podman, Slurm) and the local stack
verifier/ Replay and verification code used by the audit image
sql/ PostgreSQL migrations, applied in order
infra/ CloudFormation stacks
scripts/ Deploy, publish and live-check scripts, most of which need AWS credentials
pool/ Separate small-curve pool and STARK prototype with its own CI
problems/ Open problems with the evidence needed to close each one
verification/ Committed receipts from release checks

Set up and run the tests

You need Python 3.12+, uv and PostgreSQL 16.

uv sync --extra test
uv run python -m pytest -q

The suite starts its own PostgreSQL if initdb and pg_ctl are on PATH. initdb refuses to run as root; in that case, point the tests at a running server instead:

TEST_POSTGRES_DSN=postgresql://postgres:postgres@127.0.0.1:5432/postgres \
  uv run python -m pytest -q

Use python -m pytest, not bare pytest, so that scripts/ is importable. moto mocks S3 and SQS, so no AWS account is needed. The worker tests need no database: python -m pytest worker/tests runs anywhere. Set ECC_TEST_ENGINE to test a prebuilt engine, such as a Metal build. scripts/check_deploy.sh checks everything under deploy/ and needs kubectl, kubeconform, docker compose, systemd-analyze and shellcheck.

The local stack runs the whole platform locally: site, verifier, emulated AWS and a CPU worker uploading real points. It is the quickest way to try a gateway or worker change end to end.

Pull requests

  • Keep each PR to one change. Explain what it does and how you checked it.
  • Add or update a test for any behavior change. CI runs the full suite, cfn-lint on infra/, and builds the web, admin, audit, worker and worker-cpu images.
  • Anything that touches verification, collision handling or admission needs a test that shows the bad case being rejected, not just the good case passing.
  • Don't claim a speedup or a result without the measurement or receipt behind it. Put receipts under verification/ or link them from the PR.
  • No secrets, keys or account IDs in commits, issues or PR text.

Good places to start

  • The open problems, especially verifier throughput and sustained ingest capacity.
  • Worker kernel performance for the binary and prime field walks.
  • An independent reimplementation of the point and collision checks. A second verifier written from the spec is the best way to find bugs in the first.
  • Website and docs fixes. Templates are in src/ecc_challenges/templates/; the CSP allows inline styles only, no scripts or external assets.

Reporting a security problem

If you find a way to forge accepted work, read other contributors' data or get around key revocation, do not open a public issue. Use GitHub private vulnerability reporting instead.

Progress metrics (daily lab report)

tools/progress_metrics.py exports this repository's progress metrics as JSONL for the lab-wide daily report (/Volumes/SSD990-2/progress-metrics). It reads the committed challenge-instance registry at origin/main (override with --ref or PM_REF) and prints one sample per line: metric, value, date, problem, unit, better, kind, label, source.

  • If a PR adds or changes a benchmark, leaderboard, result file or ledger source with a number worth tracking day over day, extend the exporter in the same PR. Keep metric ids stable; a renamed id is a new series.
  • Never emit estimates. Omit expected rho work, operation counts and rates derived from distinguished points (DPs), and projected completion times. If a source is missing, emit nothing for it; a missing walk rate is not a measured zero. Omit non-finite values. Iteration totals counted from worker checkpoints stay in, because they do not depend on DP density.
  • Live gateway counts and local ingest snapshots are separate from committed repository data. Snapshot samples identify the source filename and SHA-256. An invalid Git reference is an error.
  • python3 tools/progress_metrics.py --since 2026-10-01 must finish in under a minute, use only the standard library, run no builds and never read repository data from the working tree. The optional public gateway request has a 25-second total deadline, and an unavailable gateway does not block local exports.

worker-prerequisites.html:
Install worker prerequisites

The worker skill installs the tools for your chosen setup, then continues through worker installation and checks. Give your agent the target machine and a resource limit. These steps apply to that machine, including when the agent connects by SSH.

Choose what to install

Worker setup Required on the host
Linux CPU container Docker Engine; Compose only for the Compose recipe
Linux NVIDIA container Docker Engine, a compatible NVIDIA driver and NVIDIA Container Toolkit
Native Linux CPU Python 3.10+, a C++17 compiler, curl and tar
Native macOS CPU/Metal Python 3.10+, Xcode command-line tools, curl and tar
Native Windows CPU Python 3.10+, CMake 3.21+, Visual Studio 2022 C++ Build Tools
Native NVIDIA CUDA Native build tools plus a compatible NVIDIA driver and CUDA toolkit with nvcc

Prebuilt containers include the worker's Python and build dependencies. Native workers do not need Docker. Node.js and npm are needed only for the optional npx skills add method; agents can read the public skill URL directly.

Before installing, inspect the OS version, architecture, privileges, free disk and existing workers. Reuse compatible tools. On a shared host, keep the Docker configuration and workloads: do not remove competing packages, change the default runtime, replace a working driver or restart the daemon until you know the effect on those workloads. A pending reboot or interactive installer is an unfinished setup step.

Linux: Docker Engine

Check the current Docker context and whether both client and server respond:

docker context show
docker version

Use the intended local or remote daemon throughout. For a permission error, use the administrator-approved Docker access method, such as sudo on a rootful Engine. Docker group membership grants root-level privileges, and the socket must never be world-writable. Keep the contributor's UID and GID for the dashboard recipe's key and state mounts, even if Docker itself runs under sudo.

If the Engine is absent, follow Docker's current installation instructions for Ubuntu, Debian, or the your distribution. Check for package conflicts first; a working distribution-provided Engine can stay. The example below is for a new Ubuntu or Debian host with systemd and sudo. Run it as one block, and only after confirming this is the intended machine and that it has no conflicting packages or existing Docker repository entries:

set -eu
. /etc/os-release
case "$ID" in
  ubuntu) ECC_DOCKER_DISTRO=ubuntu; ECC_DOCKER_SUITE=${UBUNTU_CODENAME:-$VERSION_CODENAME} ;;
  debian) ECC_DOCKER_DISTRO=debian; ECC_DOCKER_SUITE=$VERSION_CODENAME ;;
  *) echo 'Follow the Docker guide for this distribution' >&2; exit 1 ;;
esac
sudo apt-get update
sudo apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends ca-certificates curl
sudo install -d -m 0755 /etc/apt/keyrings
sudo curl -fsSL "https://download.docker.com/linux/$ECC_DOCKER_DISTRO/gpg" \
  -o /etc/apt/keyrings/docker.asc
sudo chmod 0644 /etc/apt/keyrings/docker.asc
printf 'Types: deb\nURIs: https://download.docker.com/linux/%s\nSuites: %s\nComponents: stable\nArchitectures: %s\nSigned-By: /etc/apt/keyrings/docker.asc\n' \
  "$ECC_DOCKER_DISTRO" "$ECC_DOCKER_SUITE" "$(dpkg --print-architecture)" \
  | sudo tee /etc/apt/sources.list.d/docker.sources >/dev/null
sudo apt-get update
sudo apt-get install -y docker-ce docker-ce-cli containerd.io
sudo systemctl enable --now docker
sudo docker version

For the Compose recipe, also install docker-compose-plugin from that Docker repository and verify docker compose version. A single dashboard container does not need Compose. For rootless Docker or a host without systemd, follow Docker's matching instructions instead of the service command above.

Linux: NVIDIA containers

Inspect the allocated GPU with nvidia-smi and check the selected image's CUDA driver requirements in the worker guide. If the driver is absent or incompatible, use NVIDIA's driver guide for this OS and GPU. Complete any required reboot before proceeding.

If GPU container support is missing, follow the signed production repository steps in NVIDIA's Container Toolkit guide. Install its nvidia-container-toolkit package, retain a protected backup of the existing Docker configuration, then configure the NVIDIA runtime:

sudo nvidia-ctk runtime configure --runtime=docker

Review the configuration change and keep unrelated settings and the current default runtime. Restart Docker within the host's maintenance scope, then verify container execution below. A prebuilt CUDA image needs no nvcc on the host. nvidia-smi on the host does not show that a container can use the GPU.

If the user asked for a gVisor or Kata runtime, use the repository's runner setup skill and the sandbox guide. Those runtimes have extra virtualization and GPU requirements, and ordinary NVIDIA container support does not show that they work.

Linux: native build tools

On supported Ubuntu/Debian hosts, install missing tools with:

sudo apt-get update
sudo apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends python3 build-essential ca-certificates curl tar
python3 -c 'import sys; assert sys.version_info >= (3, 10), sys.version; print(sys.executable, sys.version)'
c++ --version

On other distributions, use their package manager for equivalent tools. If the OS ships an older Python, install a supported one alongside it, keep the system Python, and pass the new interpreter's absolute path as PYTHON to the worker installer. The Unix installer compiles directly; CMake and Git are needed only by recipes that use them. Install the CUDA toolkit only for a requested native CUDA build, then check nvcc --version and driver compatibility.

macOS: native build tools

Use the native worker on a Mac so it can use Metal. Docker Desktop runs a Linux VM and does not expose the Mac GPU as Metal. Check the Apple command-line tools:

xcode-select -p
xcrun --find clang++

If missing, run xcode-select --install and wait for the macOS installer to finish, then repeat the checks. Install Python 3.10+ from python.org, or use brew install python when Homebrew is already available. Verify the selected interpreter:

python3 -c 'import sys; assert sys.version_info >= (3, 10), sys.version; print(sys.executable, sys.version)'
clang++ --version

Pass PYTHON=/absolute/path/to/python3 to the worker installer if the shell still selects an older Python. Run the native worker's Metal check on this machine before choosing Metal for an ongoing run. If the user wants CPU containers on macOS, install Docker Desktop, finish its first launch, start the Engine and verify docker version.

Windows: native build tools

Use Python 3.10+, CMake 3.21+ and Visual Studio 2022 or its Build Tools with the "Desktop development with C++" workload. Match the machine's architecture; arm64 hosts also need the arm64 C++ tools. Install from Python, CMake and Visual Studio Build Tools, or use an existing WinGet installation. On an x64 host missing all three:

winget install --exact --id Python.Python.3.12 --source winget
winget install --exact --id Kitware.CMake --source winget
winget install --exact --id Microsoft.VisualStudio.2022.BuildTools --source winget --override "--wait --passive --add Microsoft.VisualStudio.Workload.VCTools --includeRecommended"

Wait for each installation and check its result. Microsoft documents the C++ workload identifiers in Visual Studio Build Tools workload IDs. Reopen PowerShell to refresh PATH; use a Developer PowerShell if CMake is only available there. Check py -3 --version (at least 3.10) and cmake --version (at least 3.21) before running the native worker installer, which verifies the C++ build. Install the CUDA toolkit only for CUDA on supported x64 hosts.

If the user asks for a Windows container setup, follow Docker Desktop's Windows guide through WSL2/virtualization and first-start checks, then select Linux containers. The native worker needs no Docker, WSL or Linux VM.

Verify and continue to the worker

Take the exact image digest from the live catalog or dashboard. Set ECC_WORKER_IMAGE to cpu_worker_image for CPU or worker_image for NVIDIA, then run the matching finite check without a key or state mount:

docker run --rm --network none -e ECC_BACKEND=cpu "$ECC_WORKER_IMAGE" --check

For NVIDIA, select the allocated GPU (device 0 here) and require CUDA, so missing GPU support fails visibly:

docker run --rm --network none --gpus '"device=0"' \
  -e ECC_BACKEND=cuda "$ECC_WORKER_IMAGE" --check

For native installs, follow the worker guide, install with ECC_START=no, then run the printed worker command with --check and the chosen ECC_BACKEND. These checks need no API key or run registration. Then continue as agent setup describes: enter the key locally, set up persistent state, start one bounded worker, and verify its heartbeat and uploads. A working compiler or Docker client alone does not complete onboarding.

running-a-worker.title: Running a worker
running-a-worker.html:
Running a worker

A worker is one process that walks one curve and uploads distinguished points. It is the same program everywhere; only the packaging differs. Pick the row that matches what you have:

You have Use Files
A Linux box with an NVIDIA GPU and Docker Docker command on your dashboard
Several workers on one machine Docker Compose deploy/docker/
A Kubernetes cluster (CPU or GPU nodes) Kubernetes deploy/kubernetes/
A server without containers Native install + systemd deploy/native/, deploy/systemd/
A Mac (Apple silicon or Intel), using its GPU through Metal macOS deploy/native/install.sh, deploy/launchd/
A Windows PC (x64 or ARM64) Windows deploy/native/install.ps1
Docker, but managed by systemd systemd + Docker deploy/systemd/ecc-worker-docker@.service
Rootless Podman Podman Quadlet deploy/podman/
A university or lab cluster with Slurm Apptainer + Slurm deploy/hpc/
No hardware, a cloud GPU account Modal, RunPod or any container host scripts/modal_worker.py

The live site lists the enabled curves at /v1/campaigns. The 19 October 2026 release enables protocol 2 for all 24 curves. Existing ECC2K-130 protocol 1 workers can keep resuming their bound checkpoints.

Quickest start

If a coding agent is helping you, use agent setup and give it the worker skill. It picks the machine, installs prerequisites, handles private key entry and persistent state, and checks worker health. If Docker, Python or build tools are missing, start with installing prerequisites.

On a Mac or a Linux machine without Docker, one command downloads the source, builds the native worker into ~/.local/ecc-challenges, asks for your API key and offers to start the worker:

curl -fsSL https://ecc-challenges.com/install.sh | sh

On Windows, in PowerShell (it installs to %LOCALAPPDATA%\ecc-challenges):

irm https://ecc-challenges.com/install.ps1 | iex

Both read ECC_CAMPAIGN (default eccp-131) from the environment, for example curl -fsSL https://ecc-challenges.com/install.sh | ECC_CAMPAIGN=ecc2-131 sh, and print the command that starts the worker again. They wrap the deploy/native installers described below; the scripts are in src/ecc_challenges/install/. Run the same command to update.

Before you start

  1. Sign in at ecc-challenges.com and create an API key. Save it where only you can read it:

    mkdir -p ~/.config/ecc-challenges
(umask 077; cat > ~/.config/ecc-challenges/api-key)   # paste, then Ctrl-D

  2. Pick a curve from the catalog, for example eccp-131 or ecc2-131.

  3. Know the rules every recipe follows:

    • One state directory per worker, kept for the life of the run. The worker stores its run ID and checkpoint there and locks it. Do not share it between workers. Do not wipe it while the run is active, or the work since the last upload is lost.
    • At most 8 active runs per account. Additional keys share this limit. Closing a run releases an active slot; the lifetime run limit still applies.
    • Stop with SIGTERM and allow up to two minutes. The worker finishes the current round, uploads what it has and saves. Every recipe here is set up that way.
    • To retire a generic protocol 2 worker, let it flush pending uploads, then run it once with ECC_ACTION=close. This closes the run on the server and keeps the data directory as a record. Original ECC2K-130 protocol 1 workers do not support that action. Pausing and resuming does not require closing.

Images

Image For Architectures
ecc-challenges-worker All 24 curves on CPU or NVIDIA GPUs (Turing through Blackwell); ECC2K-130 protocol 1 resume amd64
ecc-challenges-worker-cpu Smaller CPU-only build of the same generic 24-curve worker amd64, arm64

Images are published to ECR Public under public.ecr.aws/o1a3z1g6/; that is the registry the dashboard and /v1/campaigns name. Both are also on GitHub Packages under ghcr.io/aburan28/, which avoids ECR Public's anonymous pull allowance; use a digest from the registry you pull from. The combined image includes the CUDA engine and a parallel CPU engine, so its pinned digest works on an amd64 machine with or without a GPU. The CPU-only image is smaller and also runs on arm64. Use the digest shown on your dashboard and pin it for anything long-running, so a new release does not change the code under a run.

The CPU engine in new combined builds uses every core it is given. Run one worker per machine on CPUs and set OMP_NUM_THREADS to limit threads. On GPUs, run one worker per card.

Hardware coverage

Every implemented backend handles all 24 pinned Certicom instances, including prime and binary fields through 359 bits. Acceleration depends on the backend and host:

Host Worker
Linux x86-64 CPU Combined image or CPU-only image
Linux arm64 CPU, including Graviton CPU-only image
Linux x86-64 NVIDIA GPU, Turing through Blackwell Combined image with CUDA and a compatible host driver
macOS GPU, Apple silicon or Intel Mac with Metal Native worker; Docker's Linux VM does not expose Metal
Linux AMD or Intel GPU CPU image uses the host CPU; no ROCm, OpenCL or SYCL backend is implemented
FPGA instance CPU image can use its host CPU; FPGA acceleration is not implemented

The all-curve CUDA image requires a host driver that supports CUDA 13 (Linux R580 or newer). Its CUDA 13.0 engine includes native code for the supported GPU generations and uses CUDA minor-version compatibility. The NVIDIA driver requirement check stays enabled.

An FPGA backend needs a board-specific kernel or bitstream and a host runtime. Mounting an FPGA into a container does not provide the curve arithmetic. The Docker images target Linux; native Windows and macOS workers use the same arithmetic core. A supported backend does not enable a campaign at the gateway, so check the live catalog before starting a worker that uploads.

Check a new image on your hardware

New builds include a finite offline check for all 24 curves. It needs no API key and does not register a run or alter a checkpoint. It compares lane states and distinguished points against the Python reference and tests invalid-input rejection. Each backend runs 168 checks. A GPU check runs on both the CPU and the requested GPU backend; it fails if the requested backend is unavailable.

# Use the image you built or a release that includes --check.
docker run --rm --network none -e ECC_BACKEND=cpu "$ECC_WORKER_IMAGE" --check
docker run --rm --network none --gpus all -e ECC_BACKEND=cuda "$ECC_WORKER_IMAGE" --check

Set ECC_CHECK_OUT to a new directory in a mounted writable volume to keep the inputs, outputs and a receipt that binds the results to each engine's SHA-256. Without it, the temporary artifacts are removed. These are bounded correctness checks, not throughput measurements or challenge solutions. CI checks both final images and runs the CPU image natively on amd64 and arm64. The publishing workflow requires the CPU checks and verifies that anonymous users can retrieve the published manifests.

Docker

The dashboard shows the exact GPU command, with your image digest. On an amd64 CPU host, use that same digest without --gpus all and ECC_GPU:

ECC_WORKER_IMAGE='public.ecr.aws/o1a3z1g6/ecc-challenges-worker@sha256:a347a784935a7713b204335e8316f780a5c3209d64cc372980c1b35bee9f81ba'
mkdir -p "$PWD/ecc-cpu-eccp-131"
docker run -d --restart unless-stopped --name ecc-cpu-eccp-131 \
  --user "$(id -u):$(id -g)" --stop-timeout 120 \
  -e ECC_BACKEND=cpu -e ECC_PROTOCOL=2 -e ECC_CAMPAIGN=eccp-131 \
  -v "$HOME/.config/ecc-challenges/api-key:/run/secrets/ecc_api_key:ro" \
  -v "$PWD/ecc-cpu-eccp-131:/data" \
  "$ECC_WORKER_IMAGE"
docker logs -f ecc-cpu-eccp-131

The worker runs in the background; Ctrl-C stops following its logs. Pause with docker stop ecc-cpu-eccp-131 and resume with docker start ecc-cpu-eccp-131, keeping the same container and state directory. If the name already exists, run docker start instead of repeating docker run. These match the dashboard's names. CPU workers use container and directory ecc-cpu-<challenge>. GPU workers use container ecc-gpu-<challenge>-<GPU_ID> and directory ecc-data-<challenge>-<GPU_ID>; protocol 1 runs add -dp<weight> before the GPU ID. If you started from an earlier version of this guide, keep the ecc-eccp-131 container and ecc-data-eccp-131 directory it created: a new directory registers a new run.

The digest above supports all 24 curves on CPU and CUDA and includes the OpenMP CPU engine. For the CPU-only image, including arm64, use public.ecr.aws/o1a3z1g6/ecc-challenges-worker-cpu@sha256:36b39c08cf882efe08e19fd859604a8dceff70998045b8a32c008797c5d16eb0. The dashboard shows the current pinned images.

Docker Compose

deploy/docker/compose.yaml runs CPU and GPU workers from the ECC_WORKER_IMAGE digest in .env, with a read-only root filesystem, no capabilities and your own UID, so the key file can stay mode 0600. The example digest is the amd64 CPU/CUDA image; on an arm64 host set ECC_WORKER_IMAGE to the ecc-challenges-worker-cpu digest from your dashboard. ECC_CPU_THREADS in .env limits the CPU profile's threads.

cd deploy/docker
cp example.env .env                      # set ECC_UID/ECC_GID (id -u / id -g), curve, image
install -m 0600 ~/.config/ecc-challenges/api-key api-key
docker compose --profile cpu up -d       # or --profile gpu
docker compose logs -f

For more GPUs, copy the gpu0 service to gpu1 and change ECC_GPU, device_ids and the data directory.

Kubernetes

Workers run as a StatefulSet, not a Deployment. Each replica gets its own persistent volume (data-ecc-worker-cpu-0, data-ecc-worker-cpu-1 and so on), so a rescheduled pod resumes its own run. A Deployment with a shared volume would break the one-directory-per-worker rule.

printf '%s' "$(cat ~/.config/ecc-challenges/api-key)" > deploy/kubernetes/base/api-key
kubectl apply -k deploy/kubernetes/cpu      # or deploy/kubernetes/gpu
kubectl -n ecc-challenges logs -f statefulset/ecc-worker-cpu

Edit the overlay's patch to change the curve, replicas (at most 8 per key) or the CPU limit. The CPU engine's thread count follows the pod's CPU limit. The GPU overlay requests nvidia.com/gpu: 1 per pod and needs the NVIDIA device plugin or GPU Operator. Pods run as UID 10001 with a read-only root filesystem, no service-account token and the RuntimeDefault seccomp profile.

Scaling down leaves the higher-numbered volumes in place, so scaling back up resumes those runs. To retire one for good, close its run first (see Before you start).

Native install and systemd

For hosts without containers. This needs Python 3.10+, g++ or clang++ with OpenMP, and optionally nvcc for a CUDA build.

git clone https://github.com/isogeny-labs/ecc-challenges && cd ecc-challenges
sudo deploy/native/install.sh
sudo install -m 0600 ~/.config/ecc-challenges/api-key /etc/ecc-challenges/api-key
sudoedit /etc/ecc-challenges/gpu0.env        # curve, backend, GPU index
sudo systemctl enable --now ecc-worker@gpu0
journalctl -fu ecc-worker@gpu0

The installer builds the engine on your machine, runs its self-test, puts everything under /opt/ecc-challenges and adds the ecc-worker@.service template. Each instance (gpu0, gpu1, cpu, …) reads /etc/ecc-challenges/<instance>.env and keeps state in /var/lib/ecc-challenges/<instance>. The key stays root-only; systemd passes the service a private copy. Without root, use deploy/native/install.sh --prefix ~/.local/ecc-challenges --no-systemd and run ~/.local/ecc-challenges/bin/ecc-worker yourself.

macOS

Apple silicon and Intel Macs run the native worker. The engine is built with both a CPU backend and a Metal backend, and ECC_BACKEND=auto picks Metal when the engine sees a Metal device. This needs the Xcode command line tools (xcode-select --install) and Python 3.10+ from python.org or Homebrew; the /usr/bin/python3 that ships with macOS can be older.

git clone https://github.com/isogeny-labs/ecc-challenges && cd ecc-challenges
deploy/native/install.sh --prefix "$HOME/.local/ecc-challenges"
ECC_CAMPAIGN=eccp-131 ECC_STATE_DIR="$HOME/ecc-data/eccp-131" \
  ECC_API_KEY_FILE="$HOME/.config/ecc-challenges/api-key" \
  "$HOME/.local/ecc-challenges/bin/ecc-worker"

The installer prints the engine's --probe report, which lists the Metal devices it found. It also writes a launchd agent to ~/.local/ecc-challenges/com.ecc-challenges.worker.plist; edit the curve and state directory, copy it to ~/Library/LaunchAgents/ and load it with launchctl bootstrap gui/$(id -u) ~/Library/LaunchAgents/com.ecc-challenges.worker.plist. launchctl bootout sends SIGTERM and allows 150 seconds for the worker to save. On a Mac with several GPUs, ECC_GPU is an index into the probe's metal_devices list. The Metal kernel is compiled from the same source as the CPU and CUDA engines and must match the CPU backend bit for bit on all 24 curves before it is trusted (see How each recipe was checked). For a universal (arm64;x86_64) engine or Homebrew's OpenMP, build with cmake -S worker -B build instead.

Windows

Windows 10 and 11 on x64 or ARM64 run the native worker with the CPU backend, and with CUDA when the CUDA toolkit is installed (x64). This needs Python 3.10+ from python.org and Visual Studio 2022 or its Build Tools with the "Desktop development with C++" workload (which includes CMake). In PowerShell:

git clone https://github.com/isogeny-labs/ecc-challenges; cd ecc-challenges
powershell -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -File deploy\native\install.ps1
mkdir $env:USERPROFILE\.config\ecc-challenges
notepad $env:USERPROFILE\.config\ecc-challenges\api-key    # paste the key, save
icacls $env:USERPROFILE\.config\ecc-challenges\api-key /inheritance:r /grant:r "${env:USERNAME}:R"
$env:ECC_CAMPAIGN = 'eccp-131'
$env:ECC_STATE_DIR = "$env:USERPROFILE\ecc-data\eccp-131"
& "$env:LOCALAPPDATA\ecc-challenges\bin\ecc-worker.cmd"

Stop it with Ctrl-C. The worker finishes the round, uploads and saves; cmd may then ask "Terminate batch job?", and either answer is fine. The wrapper defaults ECC_API_KEY_FILE to %USERPROFILE%\.config\ecc-challenges\api-key. Each round's checkpoint is written atomically, so a hard stop (closing the window, Task Manager, a reboot) loses at most the round in progress.

systemd with Docker

deploy/systemd/ecc-worker-docker@.service wraps docker run in a unit, with the same /etc/ecc-challenges/<instance>.env files plus ECC_IMAGE and, for a GPU, ECC_DOCKER_ARGS=--gpus all. The container runs as UID 10001, so make the key readable by that group: install -m 0640 -g 10001 key /etc/ecc-challenges/api-key.

Podman

deploy/podman/ecc-worker.container is a Quadlet unit for rootless Podman. The key is a Podman secret, delivered as an environment variable that the worker removes before starting the engine.

podman secret create ecc-api-key ~/.config/ecc-challenges/api-key
mkdir -p ~/.config/containers/systemd
cp deploy/podman/ecc-worker.container ~/.config/containers/systemd/
systemctl --user daemon-reload && systemctl --user start ecc-worker
loginctl enable-linger "$USER"

Apptainer and Slurm

Most HPC clusters run Apptainer (formerly Singularity), not Docker. deploy/hpc/ecc-worker.sbatch runs one worker per Slurm array task:

apptainer pull ecc-worker.sif docker://ghcr.io/aburan28/ecc-challenges-worker@sha256:<digest>
ECC_CAMPAIGN=eccp-131 sbatch --array=0-3 deploy/hpc/ecc-worker.sbatch

Slurm sends SIGTERM two minutes before the time limit, so the worker saves before the job ends. Each array index keeps its own state directory under ~/ecc-data, so resubmitting the same array resumes the same runs. Check your cluster's policy on long-running jobs and outbound HTTPS first.

Settings

Variable Default Meaning
ECC_CAMPAIGN set by the installers, dashboard commands and recipes, usually eccp-131; if unset, current images use ecc2k-130 Curve ID from the catalog
ECC_BACKEND auto (CPU-only image: cpu) cuda, metal, cpu, or auto (Metal on a Mac whose engine sees a Metal device, CUDA when nvidia-smi sees a GPU, else CPU)
ECC_GPU unset GPU index for this worker (CUDA device, or Metal device from generic-engine --probe)
OMP_NUM_THREADS all available cores CPU engine threads (also honored by builds without OpenMP)
ECC_LANES GPU (CUDA, Metal) 64, CPU 4 × threads; ECC2-131 and ECCp-131 (walk 4): GPU 4096, CPU 32 × threads Parallel walks. Fixed for a run once it starts
ECC_STEPS_PER_ROUND 256; ECC2-131 and ECCp-131 (walk 4): 4096 Steps between checkpoints. Fixed for a run once it starts
ECC_STATE_DIR /data Persistent state directory
ECC_API_KEY_FILE /run/secrets/ecc_api_key Key file
ECC_API_KEY unset Key as an environment variable instead of a file
ECC_PROTOCOL 2 for new state 1 only for the original ECC2K-130 GPU walk
ECC_ACTION work close retires the run in this state directory
ECC_API_URL https://ecc-challenges.com Gateway

How each recipe was checked

Every recipe except Apptainer and Slurm was run against the local stack, with uploads verified and indexed by the server:

Recipe Check
CPU image Built for amd64; engine self-test; arm64 engine cross-built and matched amd64 output on five curves under QEMU
Docker Compose docker compose config; CPU service uploaded ecc2k-95 points with read-only rootfs and dropped capabilities
Kubernetes Both overlays render and pass kubeconform -strict for Kubernetes 1.34; the pod's security settings were reproduced under Docker, including stop and resume of the same run
Native install install.sh in a clean Debian container; worker uploaded eccp-89 and eccp-97 points; SIGTERM and SIGINT stop cleanly and resume
systemd units systemd-analyze verify
Podman Quadlet Quadlet generator output checked; the same podman run uploaded eccp-109 points
Apptainer and Slurm Not run: no Slurm cluster available. Reviewed only
GPU paths Not run here (no GPU). The GPU image has its own L4 release checks in verification/
macOS (arm64, x86-64) CI Worker platforms: install.sh and CMake builds with Metal, self-test, all-24-curve CPU walk against a Python reference, Metal-vs-CPU parity on all 24 curves where the runner exposes a Metal device, universal binary, plutil -lint on the launchd agent, installed wrapper start-up
Windows (x64, ARM64) CI Worker platforms: install.ps1 under Windows PowerShell 5.1, self-test, all-24-curve CPU walk against a Python reference, file lock and atomic checkpoint, installed wrapper start-up
Linux arm64 native CI Worker platforms: as Windows, plus CMake and install.sh builds
Metal kernel source Type-checked on every CI host with clang's C++ for OpenCL, which enforces address spaces as Metal does; compiled with xcrun metal where the Metal toolchain is installed

API key activity

The private dashboard shows activity for each API key across all campaigns and worker protocols. Workers send an authenticated POST /v1/heartbeat when their work loop starts and every 60 seconds after that, independently of point discovery, long compute rounds, checkpoints and upload retries. Requests time out after 10 seconds; a failed heartbeat is retried on the next interval and does not interrupt the search. Closing a run or running --check sends no heartbeats.

A key is Active when a worker using it pinged within the past three minutes; otherwise it shows Offline. Multiple workers can share a key: stopping one does not mark the others offline. Revoked keys and suspended accounts are always offline. The status reports worker connectivity, not proof that a GPU is computing. It is calculated when the page loads; use Refresh now to update it.

Last ping is the last accepted heartbeat, by the server's clock. Last used is the last other authenticated API request that passed the key's rate limit, even if the operation was later rejected. Both timestamps are UTC. Heartbeats do not change run cursors, point counts, checkpoints or Last used.

Existing workers must be updated and restarted before they send heartbeats. For Docker, stop the worker gracefully and recreate it with the dashboard's current image, keeping the same state volume, protocol and threshold. For native installs, stop the worker, rerun the installer and resume the same state directory. No heartbeat history is inferred from earlier point uploads.

Points received sums the committed record counters for the key's runs. Re-sending a batch does not increase the count. The count includes records awaiting verification and can include repeated endpoints in different batches. It excludes unuploaded local points and unattributed historical imports. Revoked keys keep their history; unused keys show "Never" and zero points.

ECC2K-130 legacy sigma thresholds

To start a sigma run at distinguished point (DP) weight 34 that can match the old DP30 and DP32 archive, use the combined GPU image built with threshold compatibility and a new, dedicated state directory. Set:

ECC_PROTOCOL=1
ECC_CAMPAIGN=ecc2k-130
ECC_DP_WEIGHT=34

Pass these as environment variables to the worker, alongside your existing API key and state-volume configuration. This sigma implementation requires an NVIDIA GPU. The gateway advertises supported weights in /v1/config. ECC_DP_WEIGHT accepts 30, 32 or 34. DP34 is recommended for new NVIDIA sigma workers and is preselected on the dashboard. Clients use the gateway's recommended_dp_weight (currently 34) unless ECC_DP_WEIGHT is set. The chosen weight becomes part of the run and checkpoint binding and cannot be changed when resuming. Existing sigma checkpoints keep their original threshold, and old checkpoints without threshold metadata remain DP32. Pending registrations also keep their threshold across retries. Use a separate state directory when starting a different threshold.

These are Hamming-weight thresholds: DP34 emits more often than DP32. The recommendation is not a measured claim of the fastest time to a solution; GPU throughput, upload and index capacity, and continuation costs also matter. Protocol 2's dp_bits=34 belongs to a different walk and does not query the legacy archive. The operator's bounded continuation jobs described in operations can extend sigma DP34 trails to the old, rarer endpoints.

Worker health and detail pages

Open your dashboard and select a run to see its health, estimated iterations per second, latest upload, verification queue and recent batches. Each run has its own heartbeat, including when several runs share an API key. The same state directory keeps the run identity across restarts.

New workers report health every minute. After three minutes without a heartbeat, the page shows Disconnected. Computing, Upload trouble and Upload backlog are worker-reported states; upload receipts and verification results come from the gateway. Estimated iterations/s uses a 24-hour upload window and the run's distinguished point rule. It is not an instantaneous hardware measurement.

Older workers show Reporting unavailable until updated and restarted. Re-run the native installer, or use the current pinned Docker command from your dashboard, and keep the existing state directory. A key-level heartbeat cannot identify which worker is connected. For failed or quarantined batches, keep the state directory, inspect the worker logs and include the run ID when asking for help.

Dashboard counters and worker details update once a minute without replacing setup forms or newly issued keys. Use Refresh now for an immediate update. If a refresh fails, the page keeps the previous figures and labels them as unavailable.

agents.title: Set up a worker with a coding agent
agents.html:
Set up a worker with a coding agent

Give your agent the ECC Challenges worker skill and tell it which machine, challenge and resource limits to use. The skill installs missing prerequisites, including Docker and NVIDIA container support when needed. It then covers worker installation, safe restarts, health checks and troubleshooting on Linux, macOS and Windows.

Use the skill

Paste this into a coding agent that can read URLs and run commands on your machine:

Read https://ecc-challenges.com/skill.md and help me run one ECC Challenges
worker on this machine for eccp-131. Inspect existing workers first, install
missing prerequisites for the selected setup, use a persistent state directory,
and give me the stop, resume and log commands.
Use my existing hardware; ask before renting anything. Have me enter my API
key locally. Check the worker's heartbeat and explain what is still pending.

Replace the challenge, and name a CPU limit or GPU if you have a preference. Keep your API key in a private local file or enter it at the installer's hidden prompt. Do not paste it into your agent's chat.

Agents that support the Skills CLI can install the skill from this repository:

npx skills add isogeny-labs/ecc-challenges --skill ecc-challenges-worker

The Skills CLI needs Node.js and npm, but it is optional: an agent can read /skill.md directly with neither. After installing, ask the agent to use ecc-challenges-worker. In a repository checkout, the source is skills/ecc-challenges-worker/SKILL.md.

Pick a setup

Your machine Start here
Linux CPU or NVIDIA GPU The skill installs missing Docker and runtime tools, then uses your dashboard command
Mac The native installer in the worker guide, which builds the Metal backend
Linux without Docker The native installer in the worker guide
Windows The skill installs Python, CMake and C++ build tools before the PowerShell worker installer
Existing cloud or cluster allocation The matching Modal, Compose, Kubernetes, systemd or Slurm recipe

The prerequisite guide covers Docker, GPU support and native build tools, with installation commands and readiness checks. The worker guide has launch commands for each system, and the help page covers common errors. Start with one worker. Extra API keys share the account's run limits.

Check that it works

The dashboard shows worker heartbeat and health before the first point arrives. The worker logs its run ID and accepted uploads. Time to the first point depends on the curve and hardware, so ask your agent to tell apart a running process, a heartbeat, an accepted upload and a verified, indexed submission. The public status page has aggregate figures; your signed-in dashboard has your worker's details.

Keep the state directory when stopping or restarting. Docker commands use a stable container name, so docker stop NAME pauses the worker and docker start NAME resumes it. Native workers stop with Ctrl-C and resume with the command the installer printed. Allow up to two minutes for the save.

For protocol 2, ECC_ACTION=close retires a run after pending uploads are flushed; use it when you are finished with a worker. Original protocol 1 ECC2K-130 workers have a separate lifecycle. Stopping a worker temporarily does not require closing its run.
agents.skill_markdown:
---
name: ecc-challenges-worker
description: Install prerequisites and set up, inspect, resume, or troubleshoot an ECC Challenges worker on CPU, NVIDIA CUDA, or macOS Metal. Use for contributing compute to ecc-challenges.com with Docker or the native Linux, macOS, and Windows installers.
---

# ECC Challenges worker

Help the user run a persistent worker and verify its connection to the public
gateway. The worker does the curve search. You handle setup, monitoring and
recovery.

## Choose the setup

Read the current [worker guide](https://ecc-challenges.com/docs/running-a-worker)
and [live campaign catalog](https://ecc-challenges.com/v1/campaigns). The
catalog's `worker_image` and `cpu_worker_image` are the current immutable image
pins. Use the dashboard's command for the selected challenge rather than
guessing an image digest or protocol.

Before starting anything, inspect existing workers, their state directories,
and the user's chosen resource limits. Resume an existing run when possible.
Use existing hardware within the requested scope; obtain authorization before
renting capacity or increasing paid resources.

| Host | Setup |
| --- | --- |
| Linux NVIDIA GPU with Docker | Dashboard's NVIDIA command; one worker per GPU |
| Linux x86-64 or arm64 CPU with Docker | Dashboard's CPU image; usually one worker per host; set `OMP_NUM_THREADS` to the agreed CPU limit |
| macOS | Native installer. Metal uses the Mac GPU; Docker on macOS runs a Linux VM on the CPU |
| Linux without Docker | Native installer; CPU or CUDA when the toolkit is installed |
| Windows x64 or arm64 | Native PowerShell installer; CPU, or CUDA on supported x64 hosts |
| Existing managed or cloud host | Read the guide's matching Compose, Kubernetes, systemd, Slurm or cloud recipe; keep persistent storage |

Check the chosen challenge in the catalog. A solved challenge suits a
deliberate pipeline check; pick an open challenge for ongoing contributions.
The native installers default to `eccp-131`, so set `ECC_CAMPAIGN` explicitly
to keep the user's choice.

## Install missing prerequisites

Carry setup through dependency installation. The bundled
[prerequisite guide](references/prerequisites.md) has the commands and vendor
sources; if you are reading this skill at `/skill.md`, use the
[web copy](https://ecc-challenges.com/docs/worker-prerequisites). First inspect
the target host's OS, architecture, privileges, existing workers and Docker
context. Reuse working tools and install only what the selected path needs:

- **Linux Docker:** install a supported Docker Engine, start its daemon and
  verify access as the worker's user. Add Compose only for a Compose recipe.
  A Docker CLI without a reachable daemon is an incomplete setup.
- **NVIDIA Docker:** also check the host driver and install and configure the
  NVIDIA Container Toolkit. Prebuilt images need no host CUDA compiler. Verify
  the allocated GPU inside the pinned worker image with `ECC_BACKEND=cuda` and
  `--check`, so a failure shows instead of silently falling back to CPU.
- **Native Linux and macOS:** install Python 3.10+, a C++17 compiler, curl and
  tar. On macOS, finish the Xcode command-line tools setup. On native CUDA
  hosts, also install a compatible CUDA toolkit.
- **Native Windows:** install Python 3.10+, CMake 3.21+ and Visual Studio 2022
  C++ Build Tools for the machine's architecture. Finish each installer, reopen
  the terminal if needed, and verify the tools before running the worker
  installer.

A request to set up the worker includes installing its normal prerequisites on
the designated machine, within the session's permissions. Preserve daemon
settings and existing workloads. A reboot, driver replacement or Docker restart
that interrupts unrelated jobs needs maintenance approval; without it, report
that step as unfinished. Do not weaken Docker socket permissions or discard
state to get past a setup failure.

Native workers do not need Docker. Node.js and npm are needed only for the Skills
CLI; an agent can read this URL directly. Once the tools are ready, continue
through worker installation, offline checks and connection verification below.
Report missing privileges, unfinished interactive installers and unavailable
backends as they are. A dependency list alone does not complete setup.

## Credentials and installation

The user signs in with GitHub at [the dashboard](https://ecc-challenges.com/dashboard)
and creates a revocable API key. They enter the key locally in the installer's
hidden prompt or save it to the private key file
(`~/.config/ecc-challenges/api-key`). Do not ask for the key in chat, print it,
or put it in commands, logs, screenshots, commits or public issue reports. The
key does not sign an agent into the private dashboard.

On Linux or macOS, the public installer builds the worker in the user's home
directory and prompts before starting it:

```sh
curl -fsSL https://ecc-challenges.com/install.sh | ECC_CAMPAIGN=eccp-131 sh
```

On Windows, in PowerShell:

```powershell
$env:ECC_CAMPAIGN = 'eccp-131'
irm https://ecc-challenges.com/install.ps1 | iex
```

Finish the prerequisite setup above before running these installers. Set
`ECC_START=no` to install without starting a worker. In an unattended agent
session, run the printed start command after the user has saved the key. The
absence of an interactive terminal is not permission to ask for the key in
chat.

## Start and verify

For Docker, use a stable container name, `--stop-timeout 120`, the chosen
immutable image, a read-only key mount and a persistent `/data`. Follow the
dashboard's UID and GID settings so the mode 0600 key and the state directory
are accessible. Start one bounded worker before expanding.

For a new installation, `ecc-worker --check` (or the image's `--check`) runs
finite all-curve checks without credentials or run registration. The guide
covers backend selection and receipts. A pass shows correctness on the tested
backend, not production upload or throughput.

Verify registration and record the campaign, protocol, run ID, selected
backend, state directory and image digest or native version. Check heartbeat
and health in the user's dashboard. Confirm accepted uploads when they appear;
large challenges can take a long time to produce the first point, so a missing
upload alone does not mean the worker is disconnected. Dashboard health and the
archived and verified counts measure different things.

Report what was checked: installation, offline checks, running process,
heartbeat, accepted upload, and verification and index status. Name the checks
still pending. A running process alone is not a successful contribution.

## Stop, resume, and recover

- Keep one state directory per worker, campaign and protocol. Never run two
  processes on the same directory or delete it to resolve a registration,
  checkpoint, cursor, namespace or lock error.
- Stop Docker workers with `docker stop CONTAINER`; restart the same container
  with `docker start CONTAINER`. Inspect logs with `docker logs --tail 100 -f
  CONTAINER`. Keep its image and mounted state when resuming.
- Stop native workers with Ctrl-C or SIGTERM and let the current round finish.
  Restart with the same campaign, state directory and backend.
- Generic protocol 2 retires a run with `ECC_ACTION=close` once pending
  records are uploaded. Do not use it on an original protocol 1 worker. Closing
  a run retires it for good; it is not a pause.
- On 429 or 503, back off: keep pending records and let the worker retry.
  On 401 or 403, check the key file and whether the key was revoked. After a
  permanent rejection or an identity mismatch, keep the state and point the
  user to [help](https://ecc-challenges.com/help).
- Original `ecc2k-130` sigma workers use protocol 1 with their registered
  distinguished point (DP) threshold: DP30, DP32 or DP34. Generic protocol 2
  has a separate walk and state. Do not change a saved run's protocol or
  threshold to match a recommendation.
- Timeouts and unresolved server audits need operator review. They are not
  evidence of invalid points, and they are no reason to discard worker state.

For a handoff, give the user the exact restart and log commands, the state
path, resource usage and worker identity, and links to their dashboard and the
[public status page](https://ecc-challenges.com/status). Redact credentials.

modal-workers.title: Modal workers for all Certicom curves
modal-workers.html:
Modal workers for all Certicom curves

scripts/modal_worker.py reads the current pinned worker image and enabled campaigns from https://ecc-challenges.com/v1/campaigns. It refuses a disabled campaign or a campaign without protocol 2. It supports all 24 campaign IDs when protocol 2 is enabled. A real L4 passed the all-curve arithmetic controls; the final image and contributor canaries are separate release checks.

Install Modal and authenticate with modal token new. Sign in on the website, create an API key and save it as a local file readable only by you:

chmod 600 /path/to/ecc_api_key
python3 scripts/modal_worker.py start --key-file /path/to/ecc_api_key \
  --campaign eccp-131 --gpu L4 --workers 1 --hours 1
python3 scripts/modal_worker.py status --campaign eccp-131 --workers 1
python3 scripts/modal_worker.py stop --campaign eccp-131 --workers 1

Replace the campaign with any enabled ID in the catalog. CPU workers use --gpu none --backend cpu. CUDA requires a compatible NVIDIA driver and a supported GPU; the generic binary includes Turing through Blackwell targets. The preserved ECC2K-130 sigma binary is an explicit --protocol 1 path for its original compatible GPU configuration. New workers use protocol 2 by default. --workers takes 1 to 8 and --hours takes 1 to 24.

Each (campaign,protocol,worker index) has its own named sandbox and volume. The launcher keeps its state in /data/ecc-state, owned by UID and GID 10001, with private directories and mode 0600 files. Modal starts the bootstrap as root. The bootstrap resolves Modal's provider-created mount symlink, prepares the child directory, then drops privileges before running the worker. The API key is kept in an ephemeral mode 0600 file outside the persistent volume.

Volumes created by the older launcher are upgraded in place. Registration nonces, checkpoints and pending distinguished point data move into the private child directory before the worker starts. An atomic migration marker allows a bootstrap interrupted between file moves to continue. If both layouts already contain worker state, startup stops and preserves both copies for operator recovery. Do not remove either checkpoint or create another run to bypass that error.

Keep that identity to resume, and never mount one worker volume into two workers at once. Modal volumes commit asynchronously and provide no distributed file locking. The worker pins round geometry, preserves the distinguished point outbox with advanced states atomically, and can replay already admitted batches using stable batch acknowledgements after an older checkpoint is restored. Losing the checkpoint completely still requires operator recovery; the server's distinguished point archives remain intact.

The launcher sends the key as a Modal Secret and writes a mode 0600 file inside the sandbox. Keys and signed upload URLs are not logged. Revoke a key on the website to stop its access. GPU time and persistent storage are billed to your Modal account. stop keeps the volume and the server data. Start with one worker and check upload and backlog status before adding more. The account cap is eight active runs across both protocols.

The bounded, key-free python3 scripts/check_modal_volume.py --out receipt.json check verifies migration, mode 0600 ownership, atomic checkpoint writes, two fresh CPU sandboxes and external committed-volume hashes, using the exact bootstrap. Its counter data is a filesystem control. A real GPU contribution is a separate release check. Modal documents its Docker USER behavior and volume commit/locking behavior.

RunPod and other Linux container hosts use the digest shown on the website, a persistent /data volume and these settings:

Setting Value
ECC_API_URL https://ecc-challenges.com
ECC_CAMPAIGN Any enabled catalog ID, for example ecc2-131
ECC_PROTOCOL 2 for a new generic worker
ECC_BACKEND auto, cuda, or cpu
ECC_API_KEY_FILE Mounted secret path, default /run/secrets/ecc_api_key
ECC_API_KEY Provider environment secret instead of a mounted file
ECC_STATE_DIR /data, backed by a distinct persistent volume per worker

Use one key mechanism, not both. For CPU containers, omit Docker's --gpus option. The worker reads and removes the environment key before starting native code. A native arithmetic failure keeps the previous durable checkpoint and reports an error; it does not silently change the requested CUDA computation.

sandbox-runtimes.title: Kata Containers and gVisor worker checks
sandbox-runtimes.html:
Kata Containers and gVisor worker checks

The Linux worker image passed the offline CPU smoke under both gVisor and Kata Containers with the pinned published digest. The detailed receipts and host facts are in verification/sandbox-runtime-20261019. The later image advertised by the public catalog on 20 October 2026 has its own Kata and gVisor receipts. These recipes do not change public campaign enrollment. Check the live catalog before starting a worker that uploads.

Offline CPU smoke

The Sandbox worker runtimes workflow runs the gVisor smoke on an Ubuntu GitHub runner whenever this check or its overlays change. The pull-request job uses the pinned image advertised by the public campaign catalog when 24-curve enrollment was enabled and requires the complete offline 24-curve check. After a later image release, dispatch the workflow on the default branch with the new exact digest and all_curves=true. Keep the version log and the detailed receipt.

To rerun the Kata job in GitHub Actions, enroll a dedicated Linux x64 runner with the kata-kvm label, /dev/kvm, Docker 26 or newer, and the kata Docker runtime registered with the Kata runtime-rs QEMU configuration. Then dispatch the workflow with validate_kata=true and the same image digest. The job fails at preflight if KVM is unavailable. The Kata installation guide documents the Docker registration and virtualization requirements. No such runner is currently enrolled. The separate EC2 KVM smoke recorded in the verification directory does not establish that the GitHub Actions Kata job or a Kubernetes deployment works.

Use a Linux host with Docker and a configured runsc or Kata runtime, and supply the exact CPU or combined worker image digest you intend to run:

python3 scripts/check_sandbox_runtime.py \
  --runtime runsc \
  --all-curves \
  --receipt runsc-worker-check.json \
  --image 'ghcr.io/aburan28/ecc-challenges-worker-cpu@sha256:YOUR_DIGEST'
# On a host with a Docker Kata runtime, replace runsc with its registered name.

The check requires a full SHA-256 image digest and verifies that the requested runtime is registered. It runs the engine self-test and CPU probe, then writes and resumes a mode 0600 checkpoint from two separate containers running as UID 10001. With --all-curves, it also requires the image's offline --check entry point to complete at least 168 checks across all 24 campaigns. Use an image release that contains that entry point; omit the flag only to check an older image's runtime mechanics. Both containers use the same disposable named volume. The check uses no API key or network access and removes its volume when done. The required --receipt path keeps the detailed 24-curve receipt outside that volume, as a new mode 0600 file. Keep it with the Docker and runtime versions, host architecture and exit code as the evidence for a runtime-specific result. A pass establishes only CPU arithmetic and local persistence in that runtime.

Kubernetes CPU examples

The deploy/kubernetes/gvisor-cpu and deploy/kubernetes/kata-cpu overlays add runtimeClassName: gvisor or runtimeClassName: kata to the existing CPU StatefulSet. The cluster administrator must install and test the matching RuntimeClass; the names are examples and can be changed in the overlay. Before applying an overlay, replace its all-zero image digest with the reviewed CPU image digest; the placeholder deliberately cannot be pulled. The per-replica volume, unprivileged UID and 120-second shutdown grace period still apply.

After the offline smoke passes, use a private key and a canary-enabled gateway to verify one real registration, upload, audit, index, restart and closure. Keep the state volume and server receipts. Both runtimes need these steps before they can be called supported for live campaigns.

GPU boundary

The CPU overlays do not request GPUs. gVisor's NVIDIA guide requires nvproxy and a compatible host driver for CUDA. Kata's NVIDIA GPU guide uses GPU passthrough and a GPU-specific runtime class and device resource; adding runtimeClassName to the existing nvidia.com/gpu overlay is not sufficient. Test the actual GPU engine, exact curve outputs, restart, upload and drain on each configured stack before claiming GPU support.

local-stack.title: Local stack
local-stack.html:
Local stack

deploy/local/compose.yaml runs the whole platform on one machine: the website and worker API, the verification and repair workers, PostgreSQL, emulated S3/SQS/DynamoDB (LocalStack), and optionally a CPU worker. Use it to work on the gateway, the verifier or the worker without an AWS account.

docker compose -f deploy/local/compose.yaml up -d --build
docker compose -f deploy/local/compose.yaml run --rm -T init \
  python scripts/local_stack.py key me > .local-key
chmod 644 .local-key          # the worker container runs as UID 10001
docker compose -f deploy/local/compose.yaml --profile worker up -d --build worker
docker compose -f deploy/local/compose.yaml logs -f worker audit

Open https://localhost:8443 and accept the local certificate. The status page shows points arriving, then verified. The worker runs eccp-79 unless you set ECC_CAMPAIGN, and a CPU worker finds a point every few seconds on the small curves. To switch curves, stop the worker, remove its state (docker volume rm ecc-local_worker-data) and start it again with ECC_CAMPAIGN=ecc2-131 (or any catalog ID) set in your shell.

Stop with docker compose -f deploy/local/compose.yaml down. Add -v to wipe the database, archive and worker state.

How it fits together

Service Role
proxy Caddy with its own local CA. Serves the site as ecc-challenges.test and localhost:8443, and S3 as s3.us-west-2.amazonaws.com
localstack S3, SQS and DynamoDB
postgres Accounts, keys, runs, batches
init Applies sql/ (every start; migrations are idempotent), creates the bucket, queues and point table, publishes the CA certificate
web Website and worker API, with all 24 curves enabled
audit Verifies every uploaded point and queues it for the point index
reconcile Delivers queued work, repairs anything left half-done and merges the point index every 30 seconds
worker The CPU worker image, pointed at the local gateway

The worker talks only to an HTTPS gateway and uploads only to *.amazonaws.com, the same restrictions it has in production. The stack meets them with the TLS proxy and network aliases instead of relaxing the worker. Those names exist only on the stack's Docker network.

The stack uses LocalStack instead of moto because the gateway checks two things moto does not provide: the SHA-256 checksum S3 records for a signed upload, and DynamoDB's TableId.

The stack uses the compact point index (POINT_INDEX_MODE=compact, see multicurve storage). Set POINT_INDEX_MODE=dynamodb in your shell before up to use the DynamoDB index instead. To check collision handling end to end, let a worker upload a few points, then inject a known-answer collision:

docker compose -f deploy/local/compose.yaml run --rm -T \
  -v "$PWD/.local-key:/app/.local-key:ro" init \
  python scripts/local_collision_check.py eccp-79 /app/.local-key

It registers a second run, uploads one of the worker's points written with that run's own coefficients, and passes once the resolver recovers the curve's published reference scalar.

GitHub sign-in is not configured locally, so the dashboard is unusable; scripts/local_stack.py key creates keys instead. It refuses to run unless LOCAL_STACK=1, which only this compose file sets.

campaigns.title: Certicom campaigns and public status
campaigns.html:
Certicom campaigns and public status

The Certicom ECC Challenge document, updated November 2009 is the source for the 24 names, field sizes, solution snapshot and historical elliptic-curve-operation estimates in src/ecc_challenges/catalog.py. Section 4 names the challenges, section 6.1 lists the ten solutions then known, and section 6.2 gives the operation estimates. Section 6.2 mislabels the ECC2K-95 and ECC2-97 solved rows as ECC2-79; their solution dates in section 6.1 identify those rows. The website labels all of these figures as historical and does not assert that a challenge is unsolved today.

The public status page and GET /v1/status are served by this application. The database query reads the bounded run table and 16 pressure shards, and is cached for 60 seconds per web task. Runs, queue depth and total_archived_points cover this isolated public gateway only. Points imported from the earlier account (338,034,791 distinct DP32 points on 17 October 2026) are reported beside them as total_historical_points and the ECC2K-130 row's historical_points, read from the ecc_public.historical_import_totals view. The page adds them to the point totals and says so. Every new public point is matched against them. If the web role cannot read the view, those fields are null and the page falls back to gateway-only counts.

An uploaded point count is not a count of independently verified operations, so work is reported as an estimate (src/ecc_challenges/work.py). Each stored point stands for the mean walk length between distinguished points (DPs): 2^28.41 steps on the ECC2K-130 sigma walk, where DP32 means normal-basis Hamming weight <= 32 among the 2^130 even-weight x (not 32 zero bits), and 2^d for a v2 namespace pinned to d DP bits. Each walk on a curve (the sigma walk, and each pinned v2 namespace) is counted separately. Each open row carries:

  • estimated_operations_2009_log2: Certicom's estimate as a power of two.
  • estimated_work_operations and estimated_work_log2: estimated steps behind the stored points.
  • expected_operations_log2: expected steps for the campaign's default walk, sqrt(pin/(4131)) for the sigma walk and sqrt(pi*n/2) for the v2 walk, which has no automorphism quotient yet.
  • expected_work_percent and estimated_completion_probability_percent: work as a share of that expectation, and 1 - exp(-(pi/4)*(k/E)^2), the chance rho would have produced a collision by now. Separate walks on one curve add their (k/E)^2 terms.
  • points_per_hour, operations_per_second_log2 and hours_to_expected_work, over a 24-hour window.

These top-level figures count this gateway's public runs. ECC2K-130's including_historical repeats them with the imported points added to the sigma walk. The snapshot adds total_estimated_work_log2 and total_estimated_work_log2_including_historical. The estimates assume honest, random-looking walks and lag the steps still inside unfinished trails. Turning them into verified figures needs a frozen work counter with independently checked checkpoints. A Pollard rho search has no deterministic fraction complete; /pollard-rho explains the model on the site.

Contribution compatibility

The v1 path runs the ECC2K-130 Frobenius walk. Its state directory is bound to ecc2k-130; the worker sends that campaign identity to the gateway and refuses another selection. The gateway rejects v1 registration for other campaigns and returns HTTP 409 for their configuration requests. The catalog still lists them so the site shows the complete published set without admitting unverifiable data.

The same image and API key run with Docker on a local GPU, in a RunPod container, or on any host with an NVIDIA runtime, persistent /data and outbound HTTPS. The Modal guide provides the persistent state and the key through a Modal Volume and Secret. Each container needs its own persistent state directory. The dashboard pins the image by digest.

For a RunPod Pod, select that image, attach a persistent or network volume at /data, set ECC_STATE_DIR=/data and ECC_CAMPAIGN=ecc2k-130, and inject the website key as ECC_API_KEY. The worker removes that variable before launching the CUDA process. Provider settings that contain the key remain sensitive; where available, prefer a read-only mounted file at /run/secrets/ecc_api_key.

Adding a new campaign requires, in order:

  1. Import and independently check Certicom's exact field, curve, subgroup and target points; pin the parameter transcript and a known-answer test.
  2. Implement the worker walk, record format, checkpoint, and independent replay for that campaign. A name in the catalog is not an executable worker.
  3. Give the campaign its own run namespace, archive prefix, point index, collision queue, rate and storage budgets. Include the campaign and walk version in every signed or hashed identity and every database uniqueness key. No ECC2K-130 seed or orbit key can be reused across curves.
  4. Exercise one contributor end to end: key issue, registration, upload, archival, replay, indexing, collision lead and independent scalar check. Run sustained arrival and drain measurements before opening a large fleet.
  5. Mark the catalog entry's contribution ready only after those checks pass.

The pool/ prototype has a prime-field reference walk and audit ideas. Its SQLite server and generated sample curves are not a Certicom production backend. The v1 SQL schema, DP32 binary record, CUDA image, replay binary and scalar resolver are specific to ECC2K-130 and must be generalized or deployed separately for other curves. The exit gate is tracked in the multi-campaign problem record.

V2 implementation

The generic path for all 24 curves lives under src/ecc_challenges/multicurve/ and worker/generic/. See storage and validation and provider commands. The exact registry supersedes the field widths in the summary table where they disagree; Appendix A's ECCp-191 modulus, for example, has 191 bits. All v2 namespaces bind the exact instance, target and walk. The v1 routes remain specific to the original ECC2K-130 Frobenius encoding. A new empty volume selects v2; an existing state.json resumes v1 unless the operator explicitly selects another protocol. A directory from one campaign or protocol is never silently reassigned.

admission-and-capacity.title: Admission, abuse limits, and drain capacity
admission-and-capacity.html:
Admission, abuse limits, and drain capacity

Protocol scope

This service has two isolated protocols. The sections below describe the legacy ECC2K-130 DP32 path. The generic v2 path supports all 24 published Certicom instances using 56–196-byte affine coefficient records; see all-curve storage.

V2 uses tiny authenticated JSON control messages at https://ecc-challenges.com/v2/. S3 PUT capabilities bound to checksum, length, content type and encryption carry the raw bytes directly, so large uploads do not occupy web tasks. Every record must satisfy the namespace's distinguished-point (DP) predicate, curve equation and R=aG+bQ relation before any DynamoDB index write. UUID runs and hashed curve/target/walk/codec namespaces isolate the campaigns. Claimed step counts are not credited as verified work.

V2 admission limits are eight outstanding reservations and 32 pending batches per account, eight active runs across both protocols, the shared daily byte quota, and a sharded global cap, initially 512 pending v2 batches. Rejected new intents receive 429 (account) or 503 (global shard) with Retry-After; they do not obtain an upload capability. Admitted batches remain recoverable from immutable S3 objects, PostgreSQL state and receipts even if SQS delivery or a worker fails. The reconciler repairs stale unfinished work. Completed runs can be explicitly closed without recycling identity or discarding admitted data.

The audit service performs v2 verification, conditional DynamoDB indexing and collision resolution. Scaling the legacy index or resolver pools adds no v2 drain capacity. V2 capacity planning must measure complete verification and indexing per curve/record width, source-object and receipt requests, PostgreSQL coordination, DynamoDB writes and duplicates, queue age, autoscaling, and total cost. scripts/capacity.py only models legacy sampled replay and must not be used to estimate v2 capacity.
