The live single-point canaries on all 24 instances establish contribution correctness. A bounded duplicate-record backlog and recovery check establishes only its stated admission and restart behavior. Neither defines a sustained fresh-point rate or a global GPU fleet size. The configured 32-auditor maximum also depends on the account's effective Fargate vCPU quota, which is 30 until the pending request for 256 is granted. A public opening must name the measured operating envelope and keep the admission caps; autoscaling is not unlimited capacity.

Legacy protocol

The public endpoint is https://ecc-challenges.com/v1/ on an AWS Application Load Balancer in us-west-2, behind AWS WAF and two Global Accelerator static addresses. Squarespace remains the DNS provider. ECS web tasks are stateless; the dedicated private rho_dp PostgreSQL instance stores cursors and indexed public candidates, while the new account's S3 bucket holds raw batches.

Trust boundaries

Input or asset Boundary and control Meaning after control
GitHub identity OAuth callback, secure signed session, CSRF on key forms Contributor can manage only their account's keys
API key 256-bit secret shown once, HMAC digest with Secrets Manager pepper, constant-time comparison, revocation Authenticated upload principal; no cloud credential
Run ID Isolated S3 seed registry uses conditional create Seed namespace is reserved before assignment
DP upload 1 MiB body maximum, structural checks, cursor lock, immutable checksum S3 write Bytes are durably archived, not mathematically validated
Replay Post-seal random selection; first batch mandatory; exact pinned host walk Sampled record either matches, fails, or stays unverified
Collision Both trails replayed, pinned host scalar solver, separate golden-model scalar multiplication, result receipt in S3 A verified scalar requires both independent point checks

The WAF blocks more than 10,000 requests per 5 minutes from one IP, and more than 300 per 5 minutes for authentication or key routes. Both rate rules return HTTP 429 with Retry-After: 60, so shared-provider throttling is retryable rather than a permanent permission error.

The application adds these limits:

  • A 240-token per-key burst bucket refilling 4 tokens/s. A 1 MiB DP upload costs 16 tokens.
  • 5 GiB/day per key across DP batches and checkpoints.
  • Per account: any number of active keys, a combined 15 GiB/day upload limit, eight active runs and 64 lifetime run IDs.
  • One key creation per minute per account.
  • A pending-batch counter sharded 16 ways. Admission returns 503 with Retry-After when the configured backlog bound is hit.

The contributor sends a remote checkpoint at most every 15 minutes by default and pauses its GPU when the local spool fills rather than discarding unsent records.

These limits bound abuse per key and IP. They do not stop an attacker who acquires many GitHub accounts or uses many networks. WAF and per-key quotas are cost controls; the independent replay and candidate quarantine protect result integrity. A determined attacker can still consume storage and verifier capacity. Operators must watch WAF blocks, account enrollment, S3 growth, queue age, and daily AWS spend, and lower quotas or temporarily close admission if those diverge from the measured plan.

The current public run allocation is 50000..65534, or 15,535 unique run IDs over the lifetime of this campaign. IDs are never recycled because the seed is (run_id << 48) | local_counter. The lifetime account cap limits how much of that finite namespace one account can consume; operators can adjust it after reviewing contributor needs and remaining IDs. A larger contributor population needs a registry audit for additional unused IDs or a new campaign and seed format. Autoscaling HTTP tasks cannot expand the namespace.

Queue and database design

The ingest ACK follows an S3 conditional PutObject plus one PostgreSQL transaction for the cursor, quota, pressure count, and outbox row. A retry at the same byte offset and digest is idempotent; a different digest gets 409. An outbox reconciler repairs a lost SQS send after the database commit. SQS delivery may repeat, so audit, index, and resolve workers use durable status rows and unique constraints. Audit, index, and collision each have their own queue and dead-letter queue. Audit and indexing scale independently, which keeps large DP joins off the HTTP request path.

Admission checks whether a pressure shard is full before the S3 write, then atomically increments its count after the bounded write. The shard row is not locked across S3 network I/O, so unrelated runs can upload concurrently. If another upload fills it between those checks, the request returns 503; its write-once object can be reused by an exact retry after capacity clears.

The candidate index has 32 hash partitions on the 24-byte orbit key. Each index task bulk copies one sealed batch into a temporary table, joins that batch to the new account's public.distinguished_points projection through its (campaign_id,point_key) key, and inserts public candidates idempotently. That historical projection starts empty until the later verified import and backmatch; current collision lookup covers new public points against each other. The historical table is read-only to the worker role. A failed later audit marks its run's prior candidates disqualified and its leads quarantined. Source objects and audit receipts stay immutable for review.

Capacity gate

Let G be active GPUs, s measured walk steps/GPU/s, L measured mean steps per DP, B records/batch, q measured index rows/task/s, T measured seconds to replay one selected record, and R new runs/hour. Approximate rates are:

DP arrival/s       = G·s/L
batch arrival/s    = G·s/(L·B)
audit selections/s = R/3600 + max(0, batch arrival/s - R/3600)/128
index task need    = ceil(headroom · DP arrival/s / q)
audit task need    = ceil(headroom · audit selections/s · T)

Use scripts/capacity.py with measured values and at least 2× headroom. Autoscaling targets are capped at eight index tasks and 32 audit tasks. The caps protect the private RDS instance and cost; raising them needs a deliberate, measured change, not a larger queue. The service returns backpressure before the pending bound is exceeded. A queue that grows continuously at the projected peak is an admission failure even if HTTP uploads still return 201.

Before a global opening, run a sustained, production-shaped load on the release images with distinct valid run IDs and sealed DP32 objects. Record arrival and drain rates over the same interval, p50/p95 replay seconds, index rows/s, S3 request error rate, RDS CPU/IOPS/locks/connections, ECS scale events, queue visible/in-flight/oldest age, dead-letter counts, end to end bytes, and actual cloud cost. Repeat after a task restart and an injected SQS send failure. Require the queues to return to baseline after traffic stops and every acknowledged object to be indexed or explicitly retained as unverified/quarantined. Compare the measured peak to the intended GPU fleet; record the largest fleet that passed. The current DP32 replay throughput and this sustained gate are tracked in the DP32 verifier and ingest capacity problem record.

Database network boundary

The public service uses a private RDS instance in its dedicated AWS account and VPC. PostgreSQL ingress is limited to that VPC's CIDR, and both service roles use verified TLS and limited SQL privileges. The original campaign's rho-dp security group is outside this platform and remains a separate legacy exposure; it should be narrowed after a coordinated inventory of its existing ingesters. The public service has no network route or credential to that owner database.

multicurve-storage.title: All-curve distinguished-point storage
multicurve-storage.html:
All-curve distinguished-point storage

Implementation status: v2 is being integrated and is disabled by default. The production ECC2K-130 v1 walk keeps its existing encoding and namespace. A catalog entry alone never enables a worker. The ECC2K-130 v1 historical import is separate; see operations.

Scope and identities

Support covers the 24 instances in Appendix A of the official Certicom challenge document: 9 prime-field and 15 binary-field instances, with actual field widths 79–359 bits. src/ecc_challenges/multicurve/instances.json pins the PDF, extracted text, exact polynomial basis, coefficients, G, Q, subgroup order and cofactor. Recorded source normalizations are reproducible with extract_parameters.py. Probable-prime checks are arithmetic admission checks, not primality certificates.

A namespace SHA-256 binds the exact instance digest, target Q, walk, distinguished-point (DP) predicate, coefficient derivation and record codec. UUID runs and 64-bit trail IDs remove the legacy 16-bit run allocation constraint. No record crosses namespaces, including records for the same curve using different walks. The generic affine walk uses 32 deterministic nonzero G multiples; start coefficients use full-width SHAKE256 rejection sampling. Binary arithmetic uses the published polynomial basis.

Each record stores trail_id:u64le | steps:u64le | x:BE | y:BE | a:BE | b:BE, where R=aG+bQ. Widths are fixed per namespace, derived from field and subgroup sizes: 56–196 bytes for this registry. Scalars are binary, which avoids database numeric precision limits.

In walk 2, a finite point is a DP when the SHA-256 of its canonical x||y has trailing zero bits; the first hash byte selects the walk partition. V1 uses the Frobenius Hamming-weight predicate with per-run limits 30, 32 or 34, and new NVIDIA sigma runs should use 34. Those thresholds are distinct from the v2 hash-bit predicate and never change an existing run.

DP bits are set per curve (dp_bits_for in multicurve/codec.py). Walk 2 has no automorphism quotient, so a solve takes about E = sqrt(pi*n/2) steps. The rule is d = floor(log2 E) - 23, capped at 34. With up to 2^16 walks running at once, the steps left in unfinished walks stay under 1% of E, and each curve below the cap needs about 2^23.5 (~12 million) DPs. ECCp-79 gets 16 bits, ECCp-109 31, and every curve of 130 bits or more 34 (ECC2K-130 about 2^30.8 DPs, ECCp-131 about 2^31.4). The DP bit count is part of the namespace, so changing the rule starts new namespaces; existing runs keep the setting pinned in their manifest.

Walk versions

A namespace names its walk, so records of different walks never meet. Walk 2 (certicom-affine-radding32-v2, the SHA-256 walk above) is defined for every curve and stays valid: runs registered under it keep their namespace, manifest and verification. ECC2-131 and ECCp-131 register new runs under walk 4 by default (DEFAULT_WALKS in multicurve/codec.py); Namespace(campaign, walk_version=2) still builds the old namespace.

Walk Partition DP test Group
2 first SHA-256 byte of x‖y, low 5 bits trailing DP bits of the digest points
3 …-xonly-v3 ((x mod 2^64) * 0x9e3779b97f4a7c15 mod 2^64) >> 59 bits 64..64+d-1 of x are zero points
4 …-negmap-v4 as walk 3 as walk 3 classes {P, -P}

Walk 4 stores the canonical point of each class (prime: y <= (p-1)/2; binary: y <= x XOR y, since -(x, y) = (x, x + y)) and negates a and b together with the point, so a stored record still satisfies R = aG + bQ exactly. The collision rule, the scalar recovery (a1-a2)/(b2-b1) and the DP codec are unchanged; a collision of P with -P is the same stored point. A trail's b is its start's b or n - b, which check_trail accepts for walk 4 only. Because the group is halved, the ideal birthday model predicts sqrt(pi*n/4) steps; cycle handling adds work whose cost must be measured. A canonical walk can fall into short cycles; the engine detects 2-cycles and cycles that return to a periodic anchor and leaves them through a 33rd jump (the escape jump) at the cycle's smallest low 64-bit x word, so walks that share a cycle also share its exit. Cycle state is local to one engine call and does not enter any record.

Walks 2 and 3 keep the b of their start, because jumps add only multiples of G. Walk 4 may negate it. Verification checks that each DP's b matches the permitted sign of the start derived from its run ID and trail ID, which ties the DP to a server-assigned trail without replaying the walk. It does not check the trail's a or step count.

Submission and processing

flowchart LR
    C[Contributor container] -->|API key + intent metadata| A[HTTPS admission API]
    A -->|reserve quota and backlog| P[(PostgreSQL metadata)]
    A -->|short-lived signed PUT| C
    C -->|immutable bytes + checksum| S[(Versioned private S3)]
    C -->|authenticated commit| A
    A -->|HEAD size + checksum + version| S
    A -->|immutable admission receipt| S
    A -->|transactional outbox| P
    P --> Q[SQS verification queue]
    Q --> V[Bounded verification workers]
    V -->|full point relation checks| S
    V -->|conditional exact-point insertion| D[(DynamoDB point index)]
    D --> L[Collision lead + scalar verification]
    L --> S
    S --> X[Sorted compact segments / index rebuild]
  1. An authenticated upload intent reserves a byte quota and a backlog slot before issuing any S3 capability. At most one reserved intent exists at a run cursor, and at most eight exist per account. Intents expire after 15 minutes.
  2. A signed PUT fixes object key, content length, SHA-256 checksum, content type, server-side encryption and If-None-Match: *. Contributors receive no AWS credentials and cannot list, read, delete or choose archive keys.
  3. Commit reauthenticates the API key and run, checks the uploaded length and checksum with HEAD, and pins the S3 VersionId. Immutable batch and admission receipts describe the accepted bytes. Successful acknowledgment requires the admission receipt. A durable database outbox repairs interrupted queue sends.
  4. A verifier checks the raw SHA-256 and namespace binding, canonical coordinates and scalars, DP predicate, curve equation, and every R=aG+bQ relation. Only fully validated batches produce verified receipts and index writes. A lease token guards progress and terminal updates. Retry cannot skip an unfinished record or use another verifier's uncommitted progress.
  5. Each exact point uses a conditional DynamoDB PutItem with attribute_not_exists(pk) and ReturnValuesOnConditionCheckFailure=ALL_OLD. The prior witness is returned on a collision. This avoids a lookup/insert race and preserves the first immutable witness. Identical coefficient pairs are duplicate work; distinct pairs create deterministic collision leads.
  6. A batch is indexed only after all point inserts and collision leads are durable. For equal points, solve (a1-a2)/(b2-b1) mod n, then check dG=Q. A zero denominator is recorded as degenerate. All result receipts remain in S3. A retry after an index insert recreates any interrupted lead.

SQS is at least once: leases, immutable object keys and idempotent records are required. SQS depth is not an authoritative ledger. Reconciliation requeues unfinished database rows, including messages that expired or reached a DLQ.

Archive layout

public-gateway/<stream>/v2/
  namespaces/<namespace>/manifest.json
  raw/<namespace>/shard=<sha256-prefix>/runs/<uuid>/<byte-offset>-<sha256>.bin
  batches/<namespace>/<batch-uuid>/<receipt-sha256>.json
  admissions/<namespace>/<batch-uuid>/<receipt-sha256>.json
  checkpoints/<namespace>/<batch-uuid>/<receipt-sha256>.json
  verified/<namespace>/<batch-uuid>/<receipt-sha256>.json
  collisions/<namespace>/<lead-id>/<receipt-sha256>.json
  compaction/<namespace>/<segment-id>/<receipt-sha256>.json
  segments/<namespace>/<segment-sha256>.bin

Raw objects and receipts use conditional writes and versioning. Service roles have no object deletion permission. Bucket policy enforces conditional writes for v2. S3 remains the witness archive; PostgreSQL holds account/run/cursor, quota, processing and collision metadata. DynamoDB is a rebuildable online index. PostgreSQL account secrets and quota history still require database backups.

Do not create one S3 object per DP. Contributors upload batches up to 1 MiB; compaction groups verified batches into sorted segments targeting 128–256 MiB. A segment retains the source batch UUID and record ordinal for every witness, plus a manifest naming all source checksums and versions. Compaction never removes raw witnesses. Lifecycle rules may move old compact segments to cheaper storage after their minimum storage and access requirements are understood.

Compact point index

POINT_INDEX_MODE=compact replaces the DynamoDB index with sorted 16-byte entries in S3 (multicurve/pointindex.py). Uploads and verification are unchanged: workers still send full records, every record is still checked, and the raw batch stays the authority. Only the index is smaller.

public-gateway/<stream>/pointindex/<namespace>/parts/<part>-<sha256>.bin
public-gateway/<stream>/v2/pointindex/<namespace>/generation-<n>/<receipt-sha256>.json
Bytes Field Meaning
0–7 fingerprint first 8 bytes of SHA-256(x‖y), the digest the walk already computes
8–15 locator index_seq (40 bits) ‖ record index (24 bits), big-endian
  1. Indexing a verified batch only gives it the next index_seq (dp_index_seq, in PostgreSQL). Nothing is written per point.
  2. The reconcile task merges every POINT_INDEX_MERGE_SECONDS (or run python -m ecc_challenges.queues merge once). For each namespace with pending batches it reads their raw objects (version- and SHA-256-pinned), makes one entry per distinct (point, witness), and merges them into parts: 4,096 sorted files, one per value of the top 12 fingerprint bits.
  3. Each new fingerprint is looked up in its part. A shared fingerprint is resolved from the full records: the same point with another witness becomes a collision lead and is solved as before; the same witness is duplicate work, whose entry is dropped and counted as deduplicated; a different point is a fingerprint false positive (about N²/2⁶⁵ of them for N entries, so roughly 0.1 for a full ECC2K-130 solve).
  4. A generation manifest (parts, checksums, counts, leads) is written under v2/, then committed by compare-and-swap on dp_point_index, together with the batches it covers and their duplicate counts. Parts the new generation replaced are deleted; a lifecycle rule expires their old versions after 7 days. Parts live outside v2/, which forbids deletes.

The index is derived. Merger.rebuild(namespace) discards it, and the next merges rebuild it from every indexed batch. Counters are adjusted by the difference, so a rebuild leaves them unchanged. Batches indexed while the mode was dynamodb have no index_seq and stay in DynamoDB only.

Sizing: a merge rewrites every part that received entries, so its cost grows with the index (16 bytes per entry). ECC2K-130 at DP34 is about 2^30.8 entries, about 30 GB in S3 (under $1 a month) against about 1 TB of DynamoDB items. Merging the part lists is fast (30 million existing plus 1 million new entries in about 4 s of CPU); S3 transfer dominates. Below about 100 million entries hourly merges are cheap. Above that, merge daily (POINT_INDEX_MERGE_SECONDS=86400). A collision is found at the first merge after both points are indexed.

Capacity, abuse and accounting

API tasks scale behind the existing HTTPS load balancer. Direct S3 upload keeps DP bytes off web task memory and network paths. Verification and conditional index insertion scale independently from admission. Limit in-flight work per worker; do not submit an unbounded future per point. Autoscale against oldest queue age and sustained backlog, and monitor verifier rate, index throttle count, failed validation, duplicate rate, DLQs and reserved-byte utilization.

Admission stops issuing capabilities when bounded pressure pools fill and returns Retry-After. Clients retain pending records and checkpoint state, pause compute during failed upload, and retry with backoff. v1 and v2 have separately bounded pressure pools; their sum is the overall maximum. Keys share an account run cap and daily byte accounting; there is no anonymous ingestion route.

Full algebraic verification establishes a valid point relation. It does not prove the submitted path, elapsed GPU work, independence, or claimed step count. An attacker can still send duplicate valid witnesses; deduplication and quotas bound their impact. Do not convert reported steps into verified work. Progress percentages remain unknown until a declared work-verification and collision model exists. Audited walk segments or unpredictable replay challenges are a separate future scoring gate.

For capacity planning, raw bytes/day = 86400 * DP/s * record_bytes before compression and replicas. Conditional index write units/day are approximately 86400 * DP/s * write_attempts_per_DP * ceil(item_bytes/1024); failed conditions and retries also consume capacity. At 10,000 DP/s, raw records alone are 48.384–169.344 decimal GB/day across current widths. This is arithmetic sizing, not a measured ingest rate. Every-curve verification cost, provider GPU controls, and sustained end-to-end capacity must be measured before advertising a rate. Prewarm DynamoDB capacity and request quota increases for the intended launch rate; on-demand mode does not guarantee an unlimited instantaneous burst.

Required launch checks

  • Exact registry validation and all ten published scalar correctness vectors.
  • All 24 native CPU transitions checked against the independent Python group implementation, including wide limbs, identities and malformed encodings.
  • The same finite controls on a real NVIDIA GPU using the published image.
  • Presigned mutation rejection, quota/backlog boundaries, revoked keys and cross-namespace submissions, plus concurrent first-point collision controls.
  • Interrupted upload/commit/verification/indexing and expired-message recovery.
  • Archive-driven index reconstruction and compaction checksum verification.
  • Measured sustained ingest with declared DP/s, item widths, verification rate, queue-age limits, duplicates, retries, cost and headroom.

Sources: DynamoDB PutItem, S3 conditional writes, S3 HEAD checksums and versions, SQS delivery semantics, DynamoDB on-demand scaling.

Operator tools

The exact verified receipt list is an explicit bounded input, in a JSON array. Use a role scoped to the archive and the separate rebuild table. The tool checks its AWS account before any mutation. A rebuild checks every relation again, preserves every collision in S3, and emits completion only after durable leads.

python -m ecc_challenges.multicurve.archive_tool compact \
  --profile ecc-challenges-new --expected-account ACCOUNT_ID \
  --bucket ecc-challenges-data-ACCOUNT_ID --campaign eccp-131 \
  --verified-keys /path/to/verified-keys.json --max-input-mib 128
python -m ecc_challenges.multicurve.archive_tool rebuild \
  --profile ecc-challenges-new --expected-account ACCOUNT_ID \
  --bucket ecc-challenges-data-ACCOUNT_ID --campaign eccp-131 \
  --verified-keys /path/to/verified-keys.json \
  --target-table ecc-challenges-rebuild-20261016 --max-input-mib 128

Provision the destination rebuild table with the same pk string schema. The operator must compare complete source coverage and collision receipts before switching a service to the rebuilt table. Account/run metadata comes from PostgreSQL backups; the index tool does not restore OAuth or quota history. For archives beyond one 256 MiB group, run disjoint explicit receipt groups against the same destination with --resume; retain every group's completion receipt.

Verification workers bind the DynamoDB creation UUID (TableId) to a durable PostgreSQL row on their first startup, before any batch has been indexed. A table recreated under the same name fails this fence. Worker roles can insert and read the binding but cannot update or delete it. Rebuilds target a separate name; only an operator can activate a complete rebuilt generation after checking all completion and collision receipts. Stop workers during that operation.

operations.html:
Operations and release sequence

The public platform belongs in its own AWS account in us-west-2. Squarespace manages DNS for ecc-challenges.com. The original ECC2K campaign remains in account ACCOUNT_ID; do not connect the public service to its RDS instance or S3 bucket. The deployment scripts require a named AWS profile and the expected 12-digit account ID, then verify the active AWS identity before writing. Configure credentials locally and rotate any credential that was exposed. Never put a secret value in chat, a shell command, a PR, or a tracked file.

What the new account owns

  • The foundation stack: private ECR repositories, three durable queues with dead-letter queues, and generated application secrets.
  • The data stack: a dedicated VPC, a private encrypted Multi-AZ PostgreSQL instance, a versioned private S3 archive, an empty historical-point table, a GitHub App sign-in secret placeholder, and a one-off ECS administration task.
  • The service stack: HTTPS ALB, WAF rate rules, stateless web and queue workers, separate autoscaling, queue alarms, and Global Accelerator.

The historical-point table starts empty. New public uploads are archived, audited, indexed, and matched against other new public points. Matches with the original campaign's existing points are unavailable until the historical import and backmatch below have run. Leave the new index queue running: every new batch and candidate is preserved, and the backmatch covers the interval before import.

The old campaign's run registry currently has no entries in the public range 50000–65534 (read-only check on 2026-10-14). Reserve that range for the public service in both accounts. The isolated registry uses the same format but has its own S3 bucket; do not let the original allocator use public run IDs.

Historical point import

scripts/historical_import.py copies the original campaign's points into public.distinguished_points in one direction. It never connects the public service to the original account: the operator runs the export with a read-only profile for account ACCOUNT_ID, and the public database never sees that account's credentials. The original S3 dp/ corpus is the source, because the original RDS table is a derived view that can lag it.

  1. export --dry-run lists and checks the whole corpus and writes nothing. It refuses any object whose .bin.json marker or key sha256 disagrees with its body. It drops and counts records that are not canonical distinguished-point (DP) keys of weight 32 (DP32) or whose seed falls in the public run range 50000–65534. Read its summary before going on.
  2. export --parts s3://<public archive>/historical-import/<date> writes each source object as a checksum-bound part with a JSON sidecar. It resumes by skipping source keys that already have a sidecar.
  3. load runs with the database owner's DSN in HISTORICAL_DSN. Each part is re-hashed, inserted with ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING, and recorded in ecc_public.historical_import_parts in the same transaction, so a rerun skips finished parts. Two historical seeds reaching one point are kept in ecc_public.historical_conflicts; any row there is a collision in the original campaign and needs the solver.
  4. backmatch runs after the last load. Batches indexed before their point was imported never joined against it; it writes the campaign leads that index_one would have written, and the resolver picks them up as usual. It is idempotent. Run it again after any later load.
  5. reconcile (optional) compares per-worker counts with the original RDS view through a read-only SOURCE_DSN. Workers short of the source there need a look; workers ahead of it are the view lagging S3.

First run, 2026-10-17, from historical-import/20261017/: 40,309 objects exported (the 68 <sha256>-<start>-<end>.bin runner deltas included), one witness-format object refused, 189,871,706 weight-34 records dropped as above_dp32_weight. 384,765,103 records loaded in two admin-task runs, 338,034,791 distinct points inserted, 0 historical conflicts. Backmatch: 0 matches, as no public ECC2K-130 points had been indexed yet. The original fleet was still writing, so later objects need another export, load and backmatch. Export to the same historical-import/20261017/ prefix: it skips sources that already have a sidecar there, while a new prefix exports everything again.

The status page reads the import's totals through ecc_public.historical_import_totals (sql/007_historical_totals.sql), which the database bootstrap creates and grants to ecc_site_web. Run the bootstrap admin task once after merging that migration. Until it runs, the page shows gateway-only counts and logs historical import totals unavailable. The order relative to the web deploy does not matter. Each later load raises the figure within a minute, with no deploy.

Size the database before loading: every historical point is one distinguished_points row of about 90 bytes with its primary key index.

1. Deploy the foundation and private data stack

Run from a clean, committed checkout. Set up a fresh named AWS CLI profile for the new account. Check that STS reports the expected account:

aws --profile NEW_PROFILE sts get-caller-identity --query Account --output text

The first deploy creates the foundation, VPC, private database, archive, admin ECR repository and an empty OAuth secret. The scripts print resource IDs and ARNs, never secret values.

python3 scripts/deploy_data.py --profile NEW_PROFILE --account-id NEW_ACCOUNT_ID
python3 scripts/deploy_data.py --profile NEW_PROFILE --account-id NEW_ACCOUNT_ID --apply

The admin image contains the SQL migrations and database bootstrap. Publish it from the same clean commit, then update the data stack using the immutable digest that the publisher prints:

python3 scripts/publish_admin.py --profile NEW_PROFILE --account-id NEW_ACCOUNT_ID
python3 scripts/deploy_data.py --profile NEW_PROFILE --account-id NEW_ACCOUNT_ID \
  --admin-image-uri ADMIN_IMAGE_DIGEST --apply
python3 scripts/run_admin.py --profile NEW_PROFILE --account-id NEW_ACCOUNT_ID
python3 scripts/run_admin.py --profile NEW_PROFILE --account-id NEW_ACCOUNT_ID --apply
python3 scripts/init_registry.py --profile NEW_PROFILE --account-id NEW_ACCOUNT_ID --apply

The admin task runs in a public subnet with an outbound public IP. Its RDS connection stays inside the dedicated VPC and uses verified TLS. It reads the RDS managed master secret and generated role passwords through its task role, installs the public schema, grants narrow privileges, and verifies both application logins. A nonzero task exit is a failed bootstrap; inspect the /ecc-challenges/admin CloudWatch log group, fix the cause, and rerun the idempotent task. The application services must wait for a successful task.

The registry initializer writes only the new account's ready marker using a conditional S3 write. It refuses a wrong account, bucket, or incompatible existing marker.

2. Configure GitHub login and TLS

Use the public ECDLP Challenges GitHub App (slug ecdlp-challenges, owned by the isogeny-labs organization, client ID Iv23lidHKj83gpKEi74i) for contributor sign-in, with homepage https://ecc-challenges.com and callback https://ecc-challenges.com/auth/callback. The site needs only the authenticated user's numeric ID and login from GET /user; this endpoint requires no GitHub App permissions. Disable the webhook unless another feature needs it, and do not grant repository or organization permissions for sign-in. A user can authorize the app without installing it. The App ID and private key are not used by this sign-in flow.

In the new account's Secrets Manager, update ecc-challenges/github-oauth to a JSON object with client_id and client_secret from that GitHub App. Keep the client secret in Secrets Manager; never paste it into chat or source. The empty initial values make service deployment fail closed. The web flow does not request OAuth scopes because GitHub Apps use their configured permissions.

GitHub documents this sign-in flow and the permission-free GET /user endpoint.

Request an ACM certificate in us-west-2 for ecc-challenges.com and www.ecc-challenges.com. Add the certificate's DNS validation CNAMEs in Squarespace and wait until ACM reports ISSUED. DNS records for the original account's certificate do not establish validation for this new certificate. The release script checks the certificate account, region, status, and both hostnames.

3. Publish contributor and service images, then deploy

Publish the contributor image into the new account's ECR Public registry. The publisher creates the repository if needed, verifies its owner, refuses an existing tag, and prints a pinned digest. ECR Public uses the us-east-1 API endpoint even when the service stack is in us-west-2.

python3 scripts/publish_public_worker.py --profile NEW_PROFILE --account-id NEW_ACCOUNT_ID

Pull the printed digest anonymously from a fresh Docker configuration. Use that digest as NEW_PUBLIC_WORKER_DIGEST below. Build and publish the web and audit images from the same clean commit:

python3 scripts/publish_images.py --profile NEW_PROFILE --account-id NEW_ACCOUNT_ID

Read VpcId, DataBucketName, and DatabaseHost from the ecc-challenges-data CloudFormation outputs. The service deployer checks all three against that stack and checks its generated DB password secrets against the foundation. The first command is a read-only plan. Replace the placeholders with the reported IDs, certificate ARN, and image tag:

python3 scripts/deploy_service.py --profile NEW_PROFILE --account-id NEW_ACCOUNT_ID \
  --certificate-arn NEW_CERT_ARN --public-worker-image NEW_PUBLIC_WORKER_DIGEST \
  --vpc-id NEW_VPC_ID \
  --bucket DATA_BUCKET --db-host DB_HOST --tag git-COMMITSHA
python3 scripts/deploy_service.py --profile NEW_PROFILE --account-id NEW_ACCOUNT_ID \
  --certificate-arn NEW_CERT_ARN --public-worker-image NEW_PUBLIC_WORKER_DIGEST \
  --vpc-id NEW_VPC_ID \
  --bucket DATA_BUCKET --db-host DB_HOST --tag git-COMMITSHA \
  --web-tasks 2 --audit-tasks 2 --index-tasks 1 \
  --reconcile-tasks 1 --resolve-tasks 1 --apply

Add --alert-email ADDRESS to the deploy command to subscribe an operator to audit-age, index-age, and dead-letter alarms. The recipient must confirm the Amazon SNS subscription email before notifications arrive. The alert topic and alarm actions exist even when no email is configured, but an unconfirmed or missing subscription is not an alert path. Check the subscription status with aws sns list-subscriptions-by-topic using the service stack's AlertTopicArn output, and verify alarm actions before DNS cutover.

Before routing DNS, exercise the ALB with the intended hostname and TLS SNI:

curl --connect-to ecc-challenges.com:443:ALB_DNS:443 \
  https://ecc-challenges.com/health

Before cutover, require all of these: healthy web targets in both zones; GitHub sign-in and key creation; a real NVIDIA contributor container run; first-batch exact replay; indexing of new public candidates; invalid-seed quarantine; an outbox/SQS restart drill; and an anonymous pull of the contributor image. The dashboard uses the pinned public digest that the service deployer verified belongs to the new account.

The service stack outputs two Global Accelerator IPv4 addresses and its DNS name. Set both apex A records in Squarespace, point the www CNAME at the accelerator DNS name, and remove conflicting Squarespace defaults. Verify /health, login and the dashboard through ordinary DNS from outside AWS. The addresses stay stable across ALB changes.

4. Watch and respond

  • Watch ALB 5xx, ECS target health, WAF blocks, S3 errors, RDS CPU/IOPS and connections, queue age/dead-letter counts, and pressure-shard totals.
  • The oldest-audit-message alarm and all three dead-letter queues make a growing ingest backlog visible. Measure producer arrival against audit and index drain before raising admission limits.
  • Treat unverified audits and collision leads as unresolved. Preserve the write-once input and receipt, then retry after the verifier or solver is repaired. A timeout is not a negative mathematical finding.
  • If arrivals exceed sustained drain, lower contributor quotas or suspend admission after preserving queued work. Keep S3 objects, cursor rows, dead-letter messages, and candidate quarantine evidence.

Until the historical import above has run and its backmatch has finished, describe collision coverage as new-public-to-new-public only. While the original fleet is still writing, rerun export, load and backmatch to catch up; export skips source keys it has already copied.

All-curve release builds and canary gate

infra/build.yaml provisions one bounded Linux CodeBuild release builder. It clones an explicit public commit, verifies HEAD, builds the four images, runs the native self-test, and writes pinned digests to release-builds/<commit>/manifest.json in the isolated bucket. The build role can push images and write the release manifest and has no database-secret access. No contributor credential enters the build.

Deploy migration 003 and the worker and web images before enabling v2. A rollout can set MulticurveCanaryKey to the ID portion of the designated key while MulticurveEnabled=false. Only that authenticated key can use v2; public catalog availability stays unchanged, and the worker queue still processes its batches. After the combined-container, contributor and capacity gates pass, enable v2 and clear the canary parameter. Existing v1 workers stay on their bound namespace.

Retiring a generic contributor run

An ordinary container stop preserves its run for resumption. To switch a worker permanently to another challenge, stop it gracefully, then launch the same pinned image, key, campaign and state volume with ECC_PROTOCOL=2 and ECC_ACTION=close. This authenticates ownership and retires the run without removing its checkpoints, uploaded points or verification work.

The command refuses a local pending outbox; resume normal work to flush it first. An unfinished server upload intent must commit or expire before closure. Closed runs remain readable and their admitted batches continue processing. Use a new state volume for a new run. Closing releases an active slot but does not reset the account's lifetime run limit.

V2 admission and verifier scaling

--max-pending-batches is an explicit per-protocol deployment bound (initially 512), sharded across sixteen pressure rows. At the maximum 1 MiB batch size this bounds v2 pending raw payload near 512 MiB; account and daily-byte quotas apply as well. Choose the bound from measured drain time. Contributors keep their outbox and pause on a retryable refusal.

The audit pool performs all v2 relation checks and DynamoDB insertion. The separate legacy index pool adds no v2 processing capacity. Audit scale-out uses visible queue depth and CPU utilization, up to 32 tasks. Automatic audit scale-in is disabled during the initial rollout so it cannot interrupt long, in-flight verification batches. Review pending work and retained leases before reducing the pool by hand. Extra tasks can keep running after a burst, so monitor cost and tune after the sustained capacity gate.

scripts/capacity.py models the legacy sampled verifier and cannot establish v2 throughput. A production DP/s claim requires measurements of every distinct witness under the deployed curve mix and fleet size.

Switching the point index to compact S3 parts

The compact index (see Compact point index) replaces DynamoDB items with sorted 16-byte entries in S3.

  1. Update the data stack so the bucket gets the lifecycle rule for superseded parts (scripts/deploy_data.py).
  2. Run the database bootstrap so 005_compact_point_index.sql and its grant apply.
  3. Deploy the service with --point-index-mode compact and keep --reconcile-tasks 1. In compact mode the reconcile task grows to 1 vCPU and 4 GB, and merges every --point-index-merge-seconds (default 3600).
  4. Watch the reconcile log for point-index-merge lines. Each one names the namespace, the generation, the entry count and the match count.

Batches indexed into DynamoDB earlier stay there, so switch before public contribution starts. If the index is ever in doubt, call Merger.rebuild(namespace_id) from an administration task: the next merges rebuild it from the raw batches.

Public image mirrors

ECR Public gives anonymous consumers a fixed monthly data allowance. Importers that share a cloud provider's address space can exhaust it before a container starts. infra/registry.yaml supplies a public-image authentication role with no push, private-image, bucket, database or application-secret permissions. Its GitHub OIDC trust binds the repository's verified immutable IDs and the release refs.

The existing contributor-image workflow accepts an optional source_image dispatch input. It copies the exact ECR image to ghcr.io/aburan28/ecc-challenges-worker with digest preservation and checks an anonymous pull. For the first GHCR publication, the package owner may need to make the package public in GitHub's package settings. Do not advertise the mirror until the anonymous check passes. The deployment helper requires the mirror's manifest bytes to match an image digest in the isolated AWS account.

Internal Modal checks can use a mode-0600 ECC_REGISTRY_AUTH_FILE containing a temporary pull-only token. Sending that token to a third-party importer requires explicit authorization, and an automatic approval rejection does not authorize another transport. No AWS access keys belong in a contributor container. The public release must work with an anonymous provider pull.

Reusing legacy DP30/DP32 records with sigma DP34 runs

Migration 008_sigma_compatibility.sql binds each protocol-1 run to Hamming weight 30, 32 or 34. The dashboard recommends DP34 for new NVIDIA sigma workers; /v1/config advertises recommended_dp_weight: 34. The original dp_weight: 32 and registration fallback remain for older clients, and existing runs keep their registered threshold. Historical records keep their seed and may have an unknown original threshold: the weight of an endpoint alone cannot establish which stopping rule generated it. The resolver reaches the stored endpoint when that threshold is unknown, with a finite replay bound. A bound or timeout leaves the collision unresolved. Every proposed scalar is checked separately using the pinned FPGA-model arithmetic.

This applies to certicom-ecc2k130-frobenius-v1. Protocol 2 uses another walk and a hash-bit predicate; its dp_bits=34 is not this sigma DP34. Its index is separate. Within the sigma walk, weight 34 reports more frequently than weight 32 or 30. A DP34 walk can stop before the older endpoint, so direct matching alone does not reuse every older trail.

The ordinary index automatically matches DP34 uploads against imported DP30/32 endpoints. The operator can also continue selected DP34 trails to a DP32 or DP30 endpoint, without changing the contributor's checkpoint or counting a derived endpoint as another historical point:

python -m ecc_challenges.queues bridge --limit 1 --target-weight 32 \
  --max-extra-steps 16777216 --timeout-seconds 900

Run this inside the audit image with the existing worker role, archive, and DB configuration. It queues at most --limit new records (maximum 100) and processes at most that many jobs. Repeated invocations select subsequent records. Run a separate pass with --target-weight 30 for the rarer old threshold. Each job records immutable input hashes, binary hashes, its continuation, matching witnesses, independent scalar checks, and completion/budget status in S3 and ecc_public.sigma_continuations. Completed jobs check the historical index as it exists at that moment, so import and backmatch first. There is no unbounded background continuation service. Production continuation throughput and benefit are unmeasured; begin with a single bounded job.

To export directly from the old rho-dp database, give the operator a read-only SOURCE_DSN through its environment, then run:

python scripts/historical_import.py export-database --source-id rho-dp \
  --source-walk-id certicom-ecc2k130-frobenius-v1 \
  --parts s3://DESTINATION_BUCKET/historical-import/rho-dp-YYYYMMDD \
  --parts-account DESTINATION_ACCOUNT

The exporter reads a consistent snapshot in bounded chunks. It keeps canonical endpoints with weight at most 32, counts excluded records, and makes no changes to the source database. Omit --source-dp-weight when source run configuration has not established it. After export, use the existing load and backmatch commands. Duplicate points are retained once; different seeds at the same point remain collision witnesses. The website's historical totals increase only for newly inserted distinct points. Deploy the migration and role grants before the new web/audit images.

problems.html:
Open problems

Problem Status Exit evidence
DP32 verifier and ingestion capacity Open Measured exact replay and a bounded 2× arrival and drain gate on release images
All Certicom campaign workers and validation Open The optimized public worker image passed 168/168 L4 controls and is advertised live. The nine binary curves passed 63/63 with positive DP1 output. problems/dp32-verifier-and-ingest-capaci.title: DP32 verifier and ingestion capacity
problems/dp32-verifier-and-ingest-capaci.html:
DP32 verifier and ingestion capacity

Status: open. Scope: the ecc-challenges.com public ecc2k-130 admission gateway at distinguished point (DP) weight 32. It uses the pinned sigma walk, 1 MiB batches, a 1/128 audit selection for each batch after the first (made after sealing) and the dedicated private rho_dp instance.

Specific obstruction

The exact host replay binary is built and wired to a separate SQS audit pool. Two numbers are still unmeasured on release infrastructure: the DP32 replay time per selected seed, and the sustained audit and index drain rate. The CPU walk can take hundreds of millions of steps per report. Without a measured service time and a production-shaped arrival and drain test, the configured ceilings of 32 audit tasks and eight index tasks cannot justify opening to an unbounded global fleet. A growing queue would eventually trigger admission backpressure and local worker spooling. The service would stay durable but would not keep up with the offered load.

This is a resource and validation gap, not a proof that the design cannot scale. The original campaign already has DPs in its own RDS instance, but their count says nothing about this verifier or the public gateway's throughput. Historical matching stays unavailable until the separate import and backmatch; until then the public candidate index can match new points to new points only. The reserved public run range has 15,535 IDs, which also bounds the number of distinct public run identities unless the registry is audited or the format changes. The original campaign's RDS ingress is a separate security exposure outside the public platform and does not establish a throughput result.

What would clear it

  1. Capture a frozen DP32 seed and record pair from the same sigma campaign, with exact source and image digests. Replay it independently on the release audit task size. Record elapsed seconds, iterations, CPU, memory, exit status and record byte equality. Repeat across enough distinct trails to report p50 and p95, and include a timeout control and an invalid-seed control.
  2. Run a bounded load with distinct reserved run IDs and sealed batches at 2× the planned arrival rate. Over the same interval, measure S3 acknowledgments, audit and index queue age, RDS writes, locks, CPU and IOPS, the collision outbox, dead-letter counts, ECS scaling and cost. Stop arrivals and show that both queues drain to baseline with every acknowledged object accounted for.
  3. Simulate one SQS send failure and one task restart. Show outbox repair, idempotent replay and indexing, and no lost cursor or duplicate accepted key.

A pass establishes capacity only up to the tested fleet and service limits. It does not show that every unsampled point is valid or that a collision will occur by any deadline. If the queues fail to drain, the fix is a lower measured admission ceiling, more verifier capacity or a faster exact verifier, before the public cap is raised. An invalid-seed control that reaches the candidate index without quarantine blocks release until the integrity path is fixed.

Earlier design and obstruction notes are in aburan28/cryptanalysis: ecc2k130/runner/public/ADMISSION-AND-SCALE.md and problems/ecc2k130-public-gateway-activation.md. The service code and current tests are in this repository's src/, verifier/, sql/ and tests/ directories.

problems/multi-campaign-worker-and-verif.html:
Certicom multi-campaign worker and verifier

Status: open. Scope: admitting distinguished points for the 23 published Certicom exercises and challenges other than ECC2K-130 through the ecc-challenges.com public gateway.

Binary arithmetic throughput obstruction, 2026-10-19

The nine binary campaigns have integrated worker code and finite correctness controls, but the fastest shared arithmetic for sustained Pollard rho work is not established. A bounded-word, branchless binary_xtime candidate was correct on the pinned controls yet slower than the current full-width implementation on a matched NVIDIA L4 panel. All 18 long-panel candidate invocations took longer relative to their bracketing baselines; the pooled candidate/baseline full-process median was 1.208. The ten comparisons whose baseline bracket drift stayed within 1.05 had ratios 1.122–1.360. The candidate was removed from the release diff. See the insight report and raw receipts.

This observation establishes a regression for that candidate on those L4 workloads. It does not identify the cause or prove the present arithmetic optimal.

2026-10-21 CUDA bit-length update

A CUDA-only leading-zero intrinsic for bit_length passed exact worker output, distinguished-point and step replay across the nine pinned binary campaigns. Its native L4 A/B panel had 13 stable baseline brackets out of 18, all 13 favoring the candidate; the stable-pair median full-process time ratio was 0.839 and the all-pair median kernel ratio was 0.730. The identical-binary A/A control had stable-pair median 1.004 and kernel median 1.000. Native resource output reported 160 candidate registers versus 159 baseline, unchanged stack and no spills. The first PTX A/B panel also favored the candidate in 11 of 12 stable pairs. Exact commands, raw receipts, verifier, plots and PDFs are in the arithmetic selection record. The change is retained as the faster tested arithmetic for this L4 worker workload, not as an assertion of global optimality.

The exact-commit public worker image was subsequently built, checked on an L4 against all 168 archived CUDA controls, and advertised by the live gateway. The nine requested binary curves passed 63/63 of those controls, each with nonempty positive DP1 output. The web rollout completed with two healthy targets; see the published-image release record. This closes the image-publication and finite final-image correctness steps for the optimized arithmetic. It does not close the sustained nine-curve GPU contribution or complete-campaign performance obstruction.

The long DP40 timing panels emitted zero distinguished points, so their DP hash parity concerns empty outputs. A separate optimized-source L4 check passed 168 frozen CUDA controls across all 24 curves, including positive DP1 emission for every curve; 137 DP1 records were checked among the nine requested binary curves. The positive-DP report and receipt and boundary correction keep that finite correctness result separate from sustained DP40 density.

Sustained useful-step rate, point collection/submission, server verification, restart cost and other hardware remain unmeasured. The next discriminating test is a sustained nine-curve GPU canary with matched current-image controls, recording useful steps, accepted points, wall/GPU time, bytes, verifier cost and restart behavior, with an A/A control and exact output checks. A passing full pipeline comparison would support a campaign-level improvement for its measured scope; a regression would identify the stage that erased the worker gain. Only that complete comparison can establish a campaign-level gain, so this performance requirement remains open.

Current release boundary, 2026-10-16

As of 2026-10-16, all 24 published instances have CPU and CUDA workers and the v2 archive, verifier and index path. The selected published image passed 168 checks on a real L4 as UID/GID 10001. All 24 production-predicate CPU contribution checks also passed against the deployed gateway: upload, index, checkpoint resume, and explicit run closure. Exact image/source/S3-version bindings and failed attempts are retained in release evidence.

The remaining obstruction is release validation: a real GPU contribution with a persistent volume, required CI passing on the current head, and a sustained fresh-point capacity envelope. Anonymous GHCR import and all 168 L4 checks passed, and the bounded account-backlog/refusal/restart/drain check passed. The AWS account then had 30 Fargate vCPUs; request 6b9319d443fe49b882919fe6ebcfeef4QPzCozkp asks for 256. Until it takes effect, the configured 32-auditor ceiling is not available in full.

On 2026-10-16, v2 was still restricted to the designated canary key while those gates were checked. The 2026-10-21 live catalog snapshot linked above reports multicurve_enabled: true. That later operational state does not satisfy the outstanding per-curve performance measurements. Completion probability remains unavailable because coefficient validity does not verify the claimed number of trail operations. The historical database import ran on 2026-10-17; see docs/operations.md, "Historical point import".

Modal checkpoint access obstruction

After the release PR merged, a CPU-only probe of the selected public image on Modal failed to create /data/probe.tmp as UID/GID 10001 after a successful root bootstrap chown('/data', 10001, 10001). No contributor key was supplied. The failure log and receipt are preserved as the first volume-readiness attempt. The local harness reported IndexError while parsing empty stdout; the remote stderr identifies PermissionError (errno 13) as the actual checkpoint-write failure.

Modal documents that it ignores Docker USER. Its public Volume documentation does not specify whether mount ownership changes permit another UID to access the filesystem. A mount-level UID restriction is a suspected explanation, not an established diagnosis. This blocks the Modal launcher's persistence guarantee and the real GPU contributor canary; it does not invalidate the completed GPU arithmetic or Fargate contribution checks.

The next bounded diagnostic creates a private child directory as root, records ownership and modes before/after changes, and attempts atomic writes as UID/GID 10001. Acceptance requires two fresh CPU sandboxes to read and advance the same mode 0600 checkpoint as UID/GID 10001, plus an external committed-volume hash match. An access failure requires a different verified persistence mechanism; repeating chmod/chown without changed evidence is insufficient. A passing probe permits a launcher repair and the separately authorized GPU canary. Sustained fresh-point capacity remains a separate outstanding gate.

The final shared-bootstrap attempt 5 met this filesystem acceptance criterion: two fresh CPU sandboxes advanced the same mode 0600 file as UID/GID 10001, both external committed-volume hashes matched, and the original mount-root file migrated successfully. Its frozen setup SHA is 9211407a376609a5789aa62b2d2dd5ca1d41730d41ad0dd52e92fb8b55f3704a. The provider /data entry was observed to be a symlink. Resolving that trusted entry and creating a private owned child corrected access; persisted child symlinks remain rejected. The first failed production-helper attempt rejected the provider mount symlink itself; it is preserved alongside the earlier failure and successful diagnostic controls in volume-readiness evidence.

This closes the checkpoint-permission obstruction for the tested Modal image and shared bootstrap. The real GPU contribution still requires the separately requested authorization to transmit the contributor key through a runtime Modal Secret. No contributor key was sent during these filesystem controls.

Consumer-stop and queue-baseline check

The first bounded pressure attempt rejected a valid regionless S3 hostname in the harness; its held reservation was completed and indexed normally. The second attempt observed ECS runningCount 0 while the old tasks were STOPPING. Their processes still consumed records, so the intended 32-batch backlog never formed. All 33 acknowledged records subsequently indexed through normal commit replay, with no lease mutation; that recovery receipt is retained separately.

The next preflight refused a nonzero SQS in-flight count. A read-only SQL task then measured 59 indexed v2 batches, zero pending v1/v2 batches or bytes, and zero active processing leases, while SQS retained two invisible deliveries. This is a delivery-versus-work accounting distinction. The raw SQS count alone cannot establish a pending application backlog. No message was purged or deleted to make the check pass.

The corrected bounded check must wait for the exact old task ARNs to become STOPPED. Any nonzero in-flight baseline requires a fresh, source-bound read-only SQL receipt with zero unfinished work/pressure and matching queue counts. Acceptance then requires 32 new admitted records, the precise account-cap 429 on the next intent, normal restart/drain, successful retry, stable commit replay, closure and restored service/scaling settings. A final SQL snapshot checks pressure returns to baseline. This remains a duplicate-witness engineering check; sustained unique-point capacity and global 503 behavior require separate tests.

Attempt 4 met that bounded acceptance criterion. Its separate before/after SQL receipts show zero pending bytes/batches for both protocols and zero active v2 processing leases. This closes the bounded account-refusal and consumer-restart check; it leaves fresh-point capacity, global 503 and the other release gates open.

Original obstruction (preserved history)

The public CUDA image, 32-byte DP record, run ID and seed namespace, S3 registry, PostgreSQL constraints, replay program, and collision resolver implement the ECC2K-130 Frobenius walk. The other Certicom entries include different binary-field and prime-field curves. A point or seed from one of them cannot be checked by the ECC2K-130 replay program or safely indexed under its key. The separate pool/ code is a prime-field prototype with generated sample curves and a single SQLite server; it has neither the published Certicom parameters nor this gateway's durable admission pipeline.

The site now catalogs all 24 names, and the API rejects incompatible campaign registration with HTTP 409. This is a missing implementation and validation boundary. It is not evidence that the other challenges are infeasible or that a generic worker cannot be built.

Exit evidence

For each campaign to be opened:

  1. Freeze a source-linked exact parameter transcript for field, curve, subgroup, generator and target. Verify point membership and subgroup order with an independent implementation and known-answer cases.
  2. Build a worker image with a named walk and checkpoint format, and an independent replay program for that exact walk. Demonstrate a provider neutral Docker run, plus bounded runs on at least one hosted GPU provider.
  3. Isolate campaign, walk version and run identity in registration, object keys, database uniqueness, queues and collision resolution. Prove that a point submitted under another campaign cannot be acknowledged or indexed.
  4. Complete a real contributor canary: issue a website key, register, upload records, independently replay selected trails, index an eligible batch, create a controlled duplicate lead, and independently verify a scalar result. Retain exact image, source and receipt digests.
  5. Measure the release image's arrival and drain capacity at the planned fleet rate and show bounded backlog under the controls in DP32 verifier and ingestion capacity.

Passing one campaign's checks opens only that campaign. It does not transfer throughput, point validity, or solution status to the other 22.

Original implementation sequence (preserved history)

Start with ECCp-131 and ECC2-131 because they are the other 131-bit Level I entries in Certicom's 2009 document. Import the exact Appendix A parameters and validate them independently. Implement one CPU reference walk and one versioned wire envelope, then test a known-answer trail and a wrong-campaign upload against an isolated database. Bound the run to one seed range, one container, and one replayed batch before any public registration. A matching trail and refused cross-campaign upload permit the provider canary; an arithmetic mismatch returns to parameter or walk debugging. A resource failure records the environment and leaves the mathematical status open.

The campaign integration guide gives the route for each subsequent curve. Certicom source: https://www.certicom.com/content/dam/certicom/images/pdfs/challenge-2009.pdf.

Implementation evidence, 2026-10-16

The v2 implementation now includes exact parameters for all 24 instances, fixed-width affine coefficient witnesses, UUID runs, SHAKE256 full-width seed derivation, CPU/CUDA arithmetic, direct immutable S3 upload, full algebraic verification, conditional DynamoDB collision indexing, and archive compaction and index reconstruction. See storage design and frozen correctness receipts.

All 24 parameter checks and 10 published scalar controls passed. The CPU engine passed 72 transition cases; a real Modal L4 passed 168 comparisons/rejections over all 24 curves. Isolated PostgreSQL/mocked AWS controls cover valid/rejected admission, immutable retries, verification-before-indexing, crash recovery, collision scalar verification, revocation, compaction and fresh-index replay.

This record remains open under the current release boundary above. The Linux build, final-image finite GPU controls and all 24 CPU upload/index canaries have since completed. Sustained arrival/drain measurements and a declared launch fleet rate remain outstanding. Full algebraic verification does not attest claimed trail lengths; the site's completion figures are point-count estimates under an explicit model, and verified work counts remain outstanding.

Local image builds failed because Docker Desktop could not start, and the system volume reached 100% utilization. The failed test artifacts were moved intact to the project SSD, and later isolated tests use .tmp/ there. Linux release builds run through infra/build.yaml and must produce pinned image digests before deployment. No failed receipt was overwritten.

DP predicate correction

Before enabling v2, a finite control found every one of 32 sampled ECC2-79 G multiples had odd x. Raw coordinate low bits therefore cannot be assumed to supply the intended cross-curve DP density. The initial arithmetic parity tests did not require nonempty DP output for every curve and missed this operational failure. The superseded sources and receipts are preserved under verification/all-curves-20261016/raw-x-v1/.

The generic replacement uses SHA-256 of full canonical x||y for both partition selection and the DP predicate, with native job magic ECCJOB03 and a new walk namespace. SHA-256's distribution is a walk-model assumption; the release correctness gate now additionally requires finite DP1 emission on every curve. All CPU and GPU transition controls must be rerun for this exact revision. The legacy Frobenius predicate is a separate established protocol.

The corrected ECCJOB03 implementation passed the repeated 72 CPU cases and 168 real L4 comparisons/rejections across all 24 curves. Every curve's DP1 control emitted points. Evidence: verification/all-curves-20261016/cpu-job03.json, cuda-job03-l4.json, job03-controls.tar.gz and source-job03-sha256.json. A designated key-ID preview gate permits the live canary without marking v2 publicly available. The bearer value is kept outside version control.

Public image distribution limit

The combined image built successfully in CodeBuild at source aaf1dad4b7561c47639b7583d072bfb05fbe5bed. Its public ECR digest is sha256:f6333f0cf90ff080b7d49d701a2745ad821cc10abeb2fa5c43c623eb1afaf2ee. Modal app ap-IjZkwBeYyxtWpvLD9l6v0t could not import it: the registry returned toomanyrequests: Data limit exceeded before sandbox or GPU startup. The failed receipt is retained under verification/all-curves-20261016/release/. AWS documents a non-adjustable 500 GB/month anonymous consumer limit. A shared provider egress pool is a suspected explanation; the receipt does not identify which quota-accounting identity reached the limit.

This blocks a provider-neutral anonymous-pull release, not the arithmetic check. The next steps are a temporary pull-only registry identity for the internal canary and an independent public mirror. Acceptance requires an anonymous hosted-provider pull of the exact published digest, all 168 final-image controls, and the normal entrypoint contribution check. Publishing an image or successfully pulling it inside AWS does not meet that exit condition.
